ISS5220 · Research Methodology · 7 October 2026 and 16 October 2026

Qualitative analysis with NVivo

How to read a set of interviews or documents, find the patterns in them, and show a reader where each pattern comes from

Dr Roxane de WaeghMarie Skłodowska-Curie Postdoctoral FellowIslands and Small States InstituteUniversity of Maltaroxane.dewaegh@um.edu.mt
The first day, 7 October 2026, 13:00 to 15:00

The method, on paper

You learn the difference between quantitative and qualitative research, what thematic analysis is, and what a passage, a code and a theme are. You then code a published article by hand and compare your codes with a classmate's. Before you leave, you request NVivo and you choose the paper you will code on the second day.

The second day, 16 October 2026, 13:00 to 17:00

The same method in NVivo, on a paper of your own

You build an NVivo project, import the paper you chose, make codes with definitions, code passages, group the codes under parent codes and write a memo. After the break you run the queries, read the charts and export the codebook you attach to your classwork.

Sources

Lumivero. (n.d.). Windows & Mac. NVivo 15 for Windows help. Retrieved September 28, 2026, from https://help-nv.qsrinternational.com/15/win/Content/projects-teamwork/work-with-projects-windows-mac.htm

Good afternoon. My name is Roxane de Waegh. I am a postdoctoral fellow at the Islands and Small States Institute. My project, FAR-SIDS, studies how foreign aid and the money that relatives send home support households in Jamaica, Tonga and the Comoros. On the second day you will see an NVivo project in which I coded four published studies on aid and remittances with the method I teach in this module. Next year I will use the same method on my own interview transcripts from those three countries.

The module has two days. Today we work on paper. You learn the difference between quantitative and qualitative research, what thematic analysis is and how you carry it out. Then you code a published article by hand and you compare your codes with a classmate's. On the second day we do the same work in NVivo, on a paper you choose yourself, and we finish with the queries and the codebook your classwork needs. NVivo runs on Mac and on Windows. I demonstrate on a Mac and I say where Windows differs.

For the classwork you write 400 to 500 words about the paper you code in NVivo, where you explain which themes you found in the paper, what the word frequency query and the coding query showed you, and what neither query could tell you. You submit the write up together with the codebook that you export from NVivo and a screenshot of each query. We start with the difference between quantitative and qualitative research.

The first day · Two kinds of evidence

Quantitative and qualitative research

A household survey records that a family in Tonga received 2,000 pa'anga from a brother abroad last year. Is the family 2,000 pa'anga better off?

The same family in two records: the survey row the researcher filled in, and what the mother said when asked about the money.

Quantitative research

A structured survey: closed questions, fixed answer categories

The researcher writes the questions in advance and asks every household the same ones: did money arrive from relatives abroad in the last twelve months, how much, how many times. Every answer is a number or a tick. At the end the researcher can say how many households received money and how much, and can place each household above or below a poverty line.

Qualitative research

An in-depth interview: open questions, the participant's own words

The researcher sits with the family and asks: tell me about that money. The mother says her brother sent it for their father's funeral, that it went to the church and the feast within a week, and that she now owes her brother the same help when his son marries. She described her lived experiences in her own words, which provided answers to questions that the researcher never knew to ask.

Why a ministry needs both

What the ministry can do with the two records together

Both records are true. The survey places the family above the poverty line. The interview shows that the money paid for a funeral and left the family owing the same help in return. A ministry with both records can see how many families receive money and what that money is already committed to, and can plan assistance for the families the survey counts as provided for and the interviews show are not.

Quantitative research measures. The researcher decides in advance what to ask, asks every person the same closed questions, and records the answers as numbers. Qualitative research listens. The researcher asks open questions, lets people answer in their own words, and works with those words to find the meaning people give to what happened to them. The difference is not the topic, because both can study money sent home by relatives abroad. The difference is whether the answers are numbers that fit boxes the researcher drew before the study began, or words the person chose.

Take the question on the slide. A household survey in Tonga records that a family received 2,000 pa'anga from a brother abroad last year. The survey asked every household the same questions: did money arrive from relatives abroad in the last twelve months, how much, how many times. Every answer was a number or a tick, and at the end the researcher can say how many households in the country received money, how much, and which households sit above the poverty line once that money is counted as income. This family sits above it. That is quantitative research, and the left of the picture is its record of this family.

Now the researcher sits with the same family and asks one open question: tell me about that money. The mother says her brother sent it for their father's funeral. It went to the church and to the feast within a week, and the family did not choose how to spend it, because a funeral in Tonga has costs that the family cannot refuse. She also says that she now owes her brother the same help when his son marries. Nothing in the survey asked about funerals, or about what the family owes back, because the researcher did not know those mattered until the mother said so. That is qualitative research, and the right of the picture is its record of the same family. So the answer to the question on the slide is no. The family is not 2,000 pa'anga better off. The money settled one obligation and created another.

Both records are true, and they lead a ministry to opposite conclusions. From the survey alone, remittances reduced poverty in that house. From the interview, the family never had the money to spend, and when the next ceremony comes it will send money out. A ministry that plans social assistance from the survey alone would count this family as provided for.

That is why the ministry needs both records. The survey shows how many families receive money and how much. The interview shows what the money did inside one family. With both, the ministry can see which of the families it counts as provided for are in fact provided for, and plan assistance for the others.

The family on this slide was invented for today. The next slide is a published study that did both in one place, in Samoa after a tsunami. The authors counted how fast money arrived from relatives abroad, and they asked households why it arrived when it did.

The first day · One study that counted and asked

The count and the interviews in the Samoa study

After the 2009 tsunami in Samoa, most affected households had money from relatives abroad within a week. How did the relatives know to send it?

What the count shows

How many, and how fast

Le Dé and colleagues interviewed 82 households in five villages. Of the 57 households the tsunami had affected, 41 received money from relatives within a week (Le Dé et al., 2015, pp. 656 to 657).

What the interviews show

Why, and why not

Households said their relatives had seen the disaster on the news and had sent money without waiting for a call. Households in the less affected villages waited, because their relatives overseas had not heard that their village had been hit (Le Dé et al., 2015, p. 657).

Why this matters
Le Dé and colleagues argue that aid agencies plan relief as if remittances did not exist (2015, p. 654). The count says sixteen households had no money in the first week. The interviews say why: their villages were not on the news, so their relatives abroad had not heard. An agency that tells the diaspora on the first day which villages were hit gets money to those households sooner than its own relief could, and can send its first relief to the families with nobody abroad. The interviews showed that. The count could not.
Sources

Le Dé, L., Gaillard, J. C., Friesen, W., & Smith, F. M. (2015). Remittances in the face of disasters: A case study of rural Samoa. Environment, Development and Sustainability, 17(3), 653–672. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10668-014-9559-0

In September 2009 a tsunami struck the south coast of Upolu, in Samoa. Most of the affected households had money from relatives abroad within a week. How did the relatives know to send it? Give me a guess before I say anything else.

If you said a phone call, that is a sensible guess. Loïc Le Dé and his colleagues interviewed 82 households in five villages in 2012 and 2013. Of the 57 households that the tsunami had affected and that answered the question, 10 had money the same day, 14 within three days and 17 within a week, so 41 of the 57 received money within a week (Le Dé et al., 2015, pp. 656 to 657). That is the number on the left of the picture. The number tells you how many households received money and how fast.

The number cannot answer the question I asked you. The interviews can. Households explained that their relatives had seen the disaster on the news and had sent money through the usual transfer companies without waiting for a call. The same interviews explain the sixteen households that had no money within the first week. Those households lived in the less affected villages, and their relatives overseas had not heard that their village had been hit (Le Dé et al., 2015, p. 657).

Now look at what the two kinds of evidence do for an aid agency. Aid agencies plan relief as if remittances did not exist, and this study argues that remittances are part of how households respond (Le Dé et al., 2015, p. 654). The count says that sixteen households had nothing in the first week, and a count leads an agency to one answer: send relief to those sixteen. The interviews say why the sixteen had nothing: their villages were not on the news, so their relatives abroad had not heard. That leads the agency to a different answer, and a cheaper one: make sure the diaspora hears, on the first day, which villages were hit, so that relatives can send before relief arrives. The agency can then send its first relief to the families with nobody abroad, and reach the others afterwards. The count could not have produced that recommendation. The interviews produced it.

Le Dé had 82 households. The next study had forty thousand people, and it asked the same kind of question.

The first day · One study, on a very large scale

The study behind a World Bank report

If you asked people in your own community what makes a household poor, how would they describe it?

What they had

81 reports, 40,000 people, 50 countries

The study reviewed 81 participatory poverty assessments. The World Bank had held those discussions with more than 40,000 poor women and men in 50 countries during the 1990s (Narayan et al., 2000, p. 3).

How they read them

Scanned, coded and counted

The team scanned the reports into text files and coded them with QSR NUD*IST, an older qualitative analysis programme from the company that later developed NVivo. The coded passages came to just over 29,000 (Narayan et al., 2000, pp. 18, 28).

What the study found

Poverty is more than a lack of income

People described it as a lack of voice, power, independence and security as well (Narayan et al., 2000, p. 4). The World Development Report 2000/2001 drew on the study and set its strategy on opportunity, empowerment and security (World Bank, 2000, pp. 3, 6).

Why this matters
A questionnaire about income records income. The open discussions let people describe poverty in their own terms, as a lack of voice, power, independence and security as well. The World Bank could trust that finding because 29,000 coded passages stood behind it and others could check them.
Sources

Narayan, D., Patel, R., Schafft, K., Rademacher, A., & Koch-Schulte, S. (2000). Voices of the poor: Can anyone hear us? Oxford University Press for the World Bank. https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/131441468779067441/pdf/multi0page.pdf

World Bank. (2000). World development report 2000/2001: Attacking poverty. Overview. https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/673161468161371338/pdf/multi-page.pdf

In the 1990s the World Bank ran participatory poverty assessments in 50 countries. In those assessments poor women and men described their own lives in group discussions and interviews. Before I tell you what the Bank found, answer the question on the slide: if you asked people in your own town or village what makes a household poor, how would they describe it?

At the end of that decade a team led by Deepa Narayan took 81 of those reports, based on discussions with more than 40,000 people, and asked what the reports had in common (Narayan et al., 2000, p. 3). The reports were far too long to read and remember, so the team scanned them into text files and coded them. Coding means that the team gave every passage a short label saying what the passage was about. They did it in a programme called QSR NUD*IST, an older programme from the company that later developed NVivo, the programme you use on the second day (Narayan et al., 2000, p. 18). The team coded just over 29,000 passages, each one a piece of text with a label on it (Narayan et al., 2000, p. 28).

People described poverty as a lack of voice, of power, of independence and of security, as well as a lack of income (Narayan et al., 2000, pp. 3 to 4). The study was written as background for the World Bank's World Development Report 2000/2001. That report built its strategy against poverty on three parts: promoting opportunity, facilitating empowerment and enhancing security (World Bank, 2000, pp. 3, 6).

A report of that size draws on many sources, so this one study did not shape the Bank's strategy on its own. The example still matters, for two reasons. The first is what open discussions make possible. A questionnaire built around one measure, income, records income and nothing else, because the researcher decided before the first interview what mattered. In an open discussion a person can raise what matters to them, in their own words, and in fifty countries people raised voice, power, independence and security, which no income question had asked about. Their lived experience was heard because the method left room for it.

The second reason is why the Bank could trust what those discussions produced. The team did not read a handful of reports and quote the most moving lines. The report describes a systematic content analysis in which every passage was coded in NUD*IST and the codes were sorted into themes (Narayan et al., 2000, p. 18), so that every finding could be traced back to the passages it rested on. That process, reading, coding and grouping, is what you learn today, and I will refer to it as thematic analysis. The next slide defines it.

The first day · The method, named

What thematic analysis is

If you read twelve interviews and write a paragraph about what each person said, have you analysed them?

Each transcript is read for its meanings and the passages are marked. The passages are then gathered across the set, and each repeated meaning, named and defined, is a theme.

Where it sits

The foundational qualitative method

Several methods analyse words: grounded theory, discourse analysis, content analysis, narrative analysis. Braun and Clarke place thematic analysis first, because the skills it gives, close reading, coding and grouping, are the skills the other methods need (2006, p. 78).

Definition

Patterns of meaning across a data set

“A method for identifying, analysing and reporting patterns (themes) within data” (Braun and Clarke, 2006, p. 79). The search for patterns runs across the whole set of texts, not within one text (pp. 81, 86).

What it produces

Themes, with the passages that back them

A short list of themes, each with a name and a definition, the codes under each theme and the coded passages under each code, with their pages. A reader can follow any theme back to the words it rests on.

Sources

Braun, V., & Clarke, V. (2006). Using thematic analysis in psychology. Qualitative Research in Psychology, 3(2), 77–101. https://doi.org/10.1191/1478088706qp063oa

Thematic analysis is one of several published methods for analysing words. Grounded theory builds a new theory out of the data. Discourse analysis studies how people use language. Content analysis counts how often categories appear. Narrative analysis follows one person's account from beginning to end (Braun and Clarke, 2006, pp. 80 to 81, 98). Braun and Clarke place thematic analysis first among them. A researcher should learn it first, they write, because the skills it gives, reading closely, coding and grouping, are the skills every other method needs as well (Braun and Clarke, 2006, p. 78). It works on any set of texts, from interviews to published papers, and it is not tied to one theory.

Their definition is on the middle card, and you will cite it in your dissertation: a method for identifying, analysing and reporting patterns, which they call themes, within data (Braun and Clarke, 2006, p. 79). The word that matters is patterns. Thematic analysis searches for meanings that repeat, and the search runs across the whole set of texts, not inside one text (Braun and Clarke, 2006, pp. 81, 86).

That is the answer to the question on the slide. If you read twelve interviews and write a careful paragraph about what each person said, you have described them. A summary of one interview stays inside that interview. It tells the reader what one person said, in less space, and it never puts that interview beside the other eleven. Look at the picture. There are four transcripts. Thematic analysis reads each one for the meanings in it and marks the passages where each meaning appears. Then it gathers the marked passages across the four and asks how the transcripts relate: where the same meaning appears again, and where one transcript differs from the others. Three of the four carry the meaning marked in coral, relatives abroad fill the gap that aid leaves. Three carry the meaning marked in yellow, money goes first to what the household owes. Each of those, once named and defined, is a theme, and because the passages were marked, you can show a reader where each theme appears, transcript by transcript, at the level of the sentence. Four summaries cannot do that. They have no passages to point to, and they never compare.

Two habits to drop today, both from the paper. Using your interview questions as the themes, with the answers pasted under each one, is sorting and not analysis, and Braun and Clarke call it one of the worst examples of the method they have read (Braun and Clarke, 2006, pp. 85 to 86). And do not write that themes emerged from your data. The phrase hides the researcher who did the work. You identify the themes by a series of decisions, and saying so is part of the method (Braun and Clarke, 2006, p. 80).

The right card is what the process produces: a short list of themes, each with a name and a definition, the codes under each theme and the passages under each code, with their page numbers. With that list, a reader can follow any theme back to the words it rests on. Those are the three levels of the method, passage, code and theme, and the next slide takes them one at a time.

The first day · The three levels

Passage, code and theme

An examiner doubts one of your themes. Which of the three levels do you show them first?

PassageA piece of the text itself, a sentence or a paragraph, with the page or line it came from. Braun and Clarke call it a data extract (2006, p. 79). The example is from the Samoa study (Le Dé et al., 2015, p. 664). Passages are the evidence.
CodeA short name given to a passage to say what the passage is about for your research question, with one sentence saying what belongs under that name. The example is a code from the demonstration project, an NVivo project built from four studies for the second day. The passage on the left carries this code.
ThemeA group of codes with a name and a definition that make a claim about the data in relation to your research question (Braun and Clarke, 2006, p. 82). The example theme contains three codes.
How a reader checks a themeThe reader starts at the theme and reads its definition, then reads the codes under it, then opens a code and reads its passages, then turns to the page each passage came from. Every step is written down, so anybody can repeat it.
Sources

Le Dé, L., Gaillard, J. C., Friesen, W., & Smith, F. M. (2015). Remittances in the face of disasters: A case study of rural Samoa. Environment, Development and Sustainability, 17(3), 653–672. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10668-014-9559-0

Braun, V., & Clarke, V. (2006). Using thematic analysis in psychology. Qualitative Research in Psychology, 3(2), 77–101. https://doi.org/10.1191/1478088706qp063oa

The method works on three levels: passage, code and theme. Every slide from here to the activity is about one of them, so keep the three words apart. The question on the slide: an examiner doubts one of your themes. Which of the three levels do you show them first? Talk to a classmate.

Read the picture from left to right. On the left is a passage, which is a piece of the text itself, a sentence or a paragraph, with the page it came from. This one is a sentence from page 664 of the Samoa study: at the centre of this mechanism are the notions of service and obligation, tautua, from migrants toward the family (Le Dé et al., 2015, p. 664). Tautua is the Samoan word for the service a person owes their family, and the mechanism the authors mean is money sent home after a disaster. Braun and Clarke call a passage a data extract (Braun and Clarke, 2006, p. 79). A passage always carries its page, because the passage is the evidence.

In the middle is a code. A code is a short name you give to a passage to say what that passage is about for your research question, together with one sentence that says what belongs under the name. The question you code against is your research question, the question your study asks. It is not the list of questions you put to your participants, and Braun and Clarke are firm that those interview questions must not become your themes (Braun and Clarke, 2006, p. 85). Le Dé's research question was whether remittances are linked to external aid. His interview question to a household was when money arrived after the tsunami and from whom. A household that answers that money came within a day, before any aid, has said something for the research question, so that passage gets a code. A household that describes the weather that day has not, so that passage gets no code, however vivid. The code in the middle is called Kinship, reciprocity and custom, and its sentence reads: passages on family obligation, customary giving, and what is owed back. I made it for the demonstration project, the NVivo project I use on the second day, and the passage on the left carries it, because tautua is an obligation owed to the family.

On the right is a theme. A theme is a group of codes with a name and a definition, and the name makes a claim about the data in relation to your research question (Braun and Clarke, 2006, p. 82). This one is called Culture, society and agency. In the demonstration project it contains three codes: the kinship code, a code on church and religion, and a code on gender and social relations.

Now the question on the slide. The examiner doubts a theme, so you start at the theme: you show its definition, the sentence that says what the theme claims. Then you show the codes under it, so the examiner sees what kinds of passage the claim rests on. Then you open one of those codes and show its passages, with their pages, so the examiner can read the words themselves and go back to the transcript. Theme, codes, passages, page. Every step is written down, so the examiner can repeat it, and a claim that can be repeated is one an examiner can believe. The next two slides take the code and the theme one at a time.

The first day · The code

What a code is

If I gave the same page to two of you, should you produce the same codes?

A code, written properly

Kinship, reciprocity and custom

Passages on family obligation, customary giving, and what is owed back.
The name says what the code is about. The sentence says what goes under the code and what does not. Somebody else can apply this code to a new page and reach roughly the same decisions you would.

The same idea, written badly

Culture

No definition given.
This is a word and not yet a code. Six months later neither you nor your examiner can tell whether a given passage belongs under it, and a code like this collects every passage that fits nowhere else.

How long a passage isBraun and Clarke, quoting Boyatzis, say that a code names “the most basic segment, or element, of the raw data or information that can be assessed in a meaningful way” for the question (2006, p. 88). The passage is the smallest piece of text that still makes sense on its own and still says something for your research question: a phrase, a sentence or a paragraph.
Description and referenceNVivo's words, which you meet on the second day. The description is the sentence under the code name. A reference is one passage linked to one code, so a code with twelve references has been linked to twelve passages.
Why this matters
Writing the sentence takes about fifteen seconds when you make the code. Working out eight months later what you meant, across two hundred passages, can take days.
Sources

Braun, V., & Clarke, V. (2006). Using thematic analysis in psychology. Qualitative Research in Psychology, 3(2), 77–101. https://doi.org/10.1191/1478088706qp063oa

If I gave the same page to two of you, should you produce the same codes? Turn to the person next to you and agree on an answer. I will take two answers in a minute.

You should not expect to. That is not a failure. Two careful readers bring different knowledge to the same page and notice different passages in it. What the method asks is that each of you can say what your codes mean, so that a third person can see what you were doing. The sentence under the code name does that job. The two cards on the slide differ only in that sentence.

Look at the left card with me. The name is Kinship, reciprocity and custom, and the sentence says: passages on family obligation, customary giving, and what is owed back. If I hand you a new page now, you can apply that code and I can check your decisions. Now the right card. The name is Culture, and there is no sentence, so a reader cannot check anything, and six months later neither can the person who wrote it.

A code like Culture becomes the place where every passage goes that does not obviously belong anywhere else, and by the end it may contain ninety passages and mean nothing in particular. Take a passage about a son in Auckland paying for his mother's church offering. Is that culture, religion, family obligation or money? Under a code called Culture the passage goes in without a decision. Under the kinship code with its sentence you have to decide whether the passage is about what is owed to the family, and you can write that decision down. If a code in your own project grows much faster than the others, open it and read it, because it is probably doing what Culture does.

How long is a passage? Braun and Clarke, quoting Boyatzis, say that a code names the most basic segment of the raw data that can be assessed in a meaningful way for the question (Braun and Clarke, 2006, p. 88). In plain words, a passage is the smallest piece of text that still makes sense on its own and still says something for your research question. It can be a phrase, a sentence or a paragraph. Their own example is one sentence from an interview about changing your name when you marry, and that one sentence carries two codes: talked about with partner, and too much hassle to change name. My own test is whether the passage still makes sense when I read it on its own two months later.

Two words from NVivo, which you meet on the second day. NVivo calls the sentence under the code name the description. NVivo calls one passage linked to one code a reference, so a code with twelve references has been linked to twelve passages. The next slide is the theme, the level above the code.

The first day · The theme

What a theme is

Is “Money” a theme?

The percentages are shares of remittances spent in the year before the tsunami, from participatory exercises in Samoa (Le Dé et al., 2015, pp. 664 to 665).

A topic

Money

Money is the subject of the study, not a finding about it. Every study of remittances is about money, so a theme called Money makes no claim, and nothing a reader finds in your passages can support or weaken it.

A theme

A claim with codes under it

Remittances pay for what a household owes its family and church, as well as for daily needs. A reader can disagree with this sentence, and the codes and passages under it either support the claim or weaken it.

Frequency is not the test

A theme can appear in few of the texts

In Clarke's study of 26 talk shows, the six key themes appeared in between two and 22 of the 26 shows. Whether a theme is key depends on whether it captures something important for the research question, not on how often it occurs (Braun and Clarke, 2006, p. 82).

Sources

Le Dé, L., Gaillard, J. C., Friesen, W., & Smith, F. M. (2015). Remittances in the face of disasters: A case study of rural Samoa. Environment, Development and Sustainability, 17(3), 653–672. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10668-014-9559-0

Braun, V., & Clarke, V. (2006). Using thematic analysis in psychology. Qualitative Research in Psychology, 3(2), 77–101. https://doi.org/10.1191/1478088706qp063oa

Is Money a theme? Hands up for yes.

Money is a topic, and the difference matters for your dissertation, so look at the picture with me. On the left is Money. Money is the subject of the study, and every study of remittances is about money, so the word makes no claim that a reader could test against the passages. On the right is a theme built from the same Samoa study: remittances pay for what a household owes its family and church, as well as for daily needs. Under the theme are three codes, with only their names on the slide. Each code has its one sentence definition in the project, and each carries the share of remittances that households said went to it in the year before the tsunami. Fa'alavelave, which are the family ceremonies such as weddings, funerals and the bestowal of chiefly titles, took 17%, church donations took 12% and food took 13% (Le Dé et al., 2015, pp. 664 to 665).

The theme on the right makes a claim, and a reader can argue with it. Somebody could say that food, housing and school fees, at 13%, 13% and 11% on the next page of the study, together take more than church and ceremonies, so the claim is really about daily needs. You would answer by opening the codes and reading the passages under them. That argument is only possible because the theme makes a claim. Braun and Clarke put it this way: a theme captures something important about the data in relation to the research question, and represents some level of patterned response or meaning within the data set (Braun and Clarke, 2006, p. 82).

The third card is about counting, because students often assume that the theme that appears most is the theme that matters most. Braun and Clarke give an example from Victoria Clarke's own study of how lesbian and gay parents were represented on 26 talk shows. She identified six key themes, and they appeared in between two and 22 of the 26 shows. The themes that appeared in only two shows were still key, because together the six captured how the parents were presented as normal families, which was the research question (Braun and Clarke, 2006, p. 82). Whether a group of codes is a theme is a judgement about what matters for the question, not a count.

Two more examples, so that you can recognise the difference in your own work. Tourism is a topic. Young people in Gozo leave hotel work for jobs in Malta because the wages are higher is a theme, and it may turn out to be wrong. Hurricanes is a topic. After a hurricane, Jamaican households turn to relatives abroad before they turn to the government is a theme. Each of those claims can be checked against passages. You now know the three levels: passage, code and theme. The rest of the method is how you get from passages to themes. Braun and Clarke describe it as four decisions you make before you start, followed by six phases of work, and the next slide is the four decisions.

The first day · Four decisions

Four decisions you make before you code

You have read three interviews and a theory paper. Will your codes come from the interviews, or from the theory?

Each row is one decision: the question, the two choices Braun and Clarke describe, and the sentence that states your decision in your methods chapter. Square brackets are what you fill in. The sentences show the second choice in rows 1 and 2 and the first choice in rows 3 and 4, which is the usual pattern in a dissertation built on interviews.

Why this matters
Braun and Clarke say that an analyst makes four decisions before coding. When you write your methods chapter, state all four, because an examiner cannot otherwise tell which of your themes came from the interviews and which came from the theory you read before coding, and their checklist for a good analysis asks for the four to be stated (2006, pp. 81 to 86, 96).
Sources

Braun, V., & Clarke, V. (2006). Using thematic analysis in psychology. Qualitative Research in Psychology, 3(2), 77–101. https://doi.org/10.1191/1478088706qp063oa

Le Dé, L., Gaillard, J. C., Friesen, W., & Smith, F. M. (2015). Remittances in the face of disasters: A case study of rural Samoa. Environment, Development and Sustainability, 17(3), 653–672. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10668-014-9559-0

Pretorius, L. (2024). Demystifying research paradigms: Navigating ontology, epistemology, and axiology in research. The Qualitative Report, 29(10), 2698–2715. https://doi.org/10.46743/2160-3715/2024.7632

You have read three interviews and a theory paper. Will your codes come from the interviews, or from the theory? Talk to a classmate for thirty seconds. Braun and Clarke say that an analyst makes four decisions before coding (Braun and Clarke, 2006, pp. 81 to 86). When you write your methods chapter, state all four, because an examiner who does not know them cannot tell which of your themes came from the interviews and which came from the theory you read before coding. Each row of the table is one decision. The first column is the question, the middle columns are the two choices Braun and Clarke describe, and the last column is the sentence that states your decision in your methods chapter, with square brackets for what you fill in. Four decisions, four sentences. I take the decisions one at a time, and for each one I use the Samoa study as the worked example. The paper states its first decision; the other three I inferred from how the authors describe their method and present their findings, and I say so each time, because a reader of your own chapter should never have to infer.

The first decision is how much of the interviews you report. You can report every topic the participants raised, which Braun and Clarke call a rich description of the entire data set, or you can report one topic in detail and leave the other topics out, which they call a detailed account of one theme (Braun and Clarke, 2006, p. 83). Le Dé and his colleagues interviewed 82 households about how they lived through the tsunami, and the households talked about housing, food, church, work and family. The paper reports one of those topics in detail, remittances, and says so in its first paragraph: the study investigates the role of remittances in households' response to disasters (Le Dé et al., 2015, p. 653). That is the second choice in the first row, one topic in detail, and it is the usual choice in a dissertation with a word limit. If your twelve interviews are about life after a cyclone in Tonga, you can report every topic the households raised, or you can report one topic in detail, say how they rebuilt their houses. Both are legitimate. Your methods chapter says which you chose.

The second decision is where your codes come from, which is my question to you. Inductive means from the particular to the general. You read the interviews first, and each time a passage says something for your research question you write a code for it, so the codes come from the passages. For example, a household in the Samoa study says: we could count on our family overseas. You read that sentence, you decide that it answers your question, and you write a code next to it, relatives abroad helped. Nothing told you to look for that idea. The sentence itself gave it to you. Deductive means from the general to the particular. You start from the theory you have read, you write a list of codes from it before you open the interviews, and you look for each code in the passages. The Samoa authors read their interviews through the sustainable livelihoods framework (Le Dé et al., 2015, p. 656), so a reader coding deductively from that framework would arrive with codes such as resources, coping and recovery, and would code the same sentence, we could count on our family overseas, to the code coping, because coping was already on the list. Braun and Clarke describe both and note that the deductive form is sometimes called theoretical thematic analysis (Braun and Clarke, 2006, pp. 83 to 84). Now what happens in practice. You have spent a semester reading, so you arrive at your first interview with ideas and patterns already in your head, and as you read, your mind is searching for those patterns whether or not a list of codes is on the desk in front of you. Braun and Clarke say this plainly: a researcher cannot free themselves of their theoretical commitments, and data are not coded in an epistemological vacuum (Braun and Clarke, 2006, p. 84). So a code that matches an idea from your reading is a deductive code, even if you never wrote the list down. When a passage says something that your reading has no idea for, that is a new code, and it is inductive. Most dissertations use both kinds, and the honest methods chapter says so and names the theory the deductive codes came from.

The third decision is the level you code at. Semantic coding names what a passage says on its surface. Latent coding names the idea underneath it (Braun and Clarke, 2006, p. 84). Take the Samoan villager who says we could count on our family overseas. On the surface that passage describes help from relatives, and a semantic code says so. Underneath, it may describe an obligation, the cultural obligation the authors call tautua, and a latent code says that instead. Most codes are semantic, and that is not a weakness. The interpretation comes later, when you write. Your results chapter reports what you found, in the participants' words, as plainly as you can, because you do not want to change what people said. Your analysis chapter is where you ask what each finding means against the existing literature, and that is where you reach the ideas underneath a code, from the perspectives of other researchers as well as your own. Braun and Clarke describe the same movement: from description, where the data have been organised to show patterns in what was said, to interpretation, where you theorise what those patterns mean, often in relation to previous literature (Braun and Clarke, 2006, p. 84). The Samoa paper works this way. Its findings sections report what households said about speed, channels and uses, and the interpretation, that remitters send out of tautua rather than to invest, is made in the discussion (Le Dé et al., 2015, pp. 657 to 665). Remember, when you write your methods chapter, clearly state which level you coded at.

The fourth decision is your epistemology, which is what you believe knowledge is and how a researcher can get it (Braun and Clarke, 2006, p. 85). Braun and Clarke describe two epistemologies for thematic analysis. An essentialist epistemology, which they also call realist, says that a person's words report their experiences and meanings, so the researcher can report what happened to that person. A constructionist epistemology says that experiences and meanings are produced by the ways of speaking in a society, so a person's words are shaped by that society before the researcher hears them (Braun and Clarke, 2006, pp. 81, 85). Under an essentialist epistemology, you use the interview as evidence about the person who spoke. Under a constructionist epistemology, you use the interview as evidence about the society that person belongs to. Take one sentence from an interview in Tonga: I had to send money for my father's funeral. Under an essentialist epistemology, that sentence reports something that happened. This woman sent the money. She felt she had no choice. Your analysis asks why she felt that, what the money cost her household, what she expected from her family in return. You study the person. Her words are your evidence about her. Under a constructionist epistemology, that sentence shows how people in Tonga are expected to speak about family and money. Obligation to family and church is the accepted way to explain sending money, so a woman says I had to, because saying I chose not to would be shameful. Your analysis asks where that expectation comes from and what it does, for example whether it keeps money flowing from Auckland to Nuku'alofa even when a sender cannot afford it. You study the society. Her words are your evidence about it (Braun and Clarke, 2006, p. 85). Both epistemologies are legitimate. An essentialist findings chapter is about people. A constructionist findings chapter is about the society that shapes what people can say. Explain how you perceive knowledge by describing your epistemological position. This will help your examiner understand how you interpreted your findings: as claims about the people you interviewed, or as claims about the society they live in. Once the four decisions are made and written down, the analysis runs in six phases. The next slide sets them out. (Your research design chapter also states your ontology, what you believe reality is. An essentialist epistemology sits with a realist ontology, one reality that exists whether or not anyone describes it. A constructionist epistemology sits with a relativist ontology, a reality shaped by the experience of each person and each society (Pretorius, 2024, p. 2699).)

The first day · The six phases

The six phases

Which of these six phases do you think takes the longest, and which do you think is most often skipped?

The six phases of Braun and Clarke (2006, pp. 87 to 93), what you do in each and what you have at the end of it.

Phase four, in plain words

Read every passage under each candidate theme

For each candidate theme you read every passage under it and ask whether the passage belongs there. Then you reread the whole set of texts to see whether you missed a passage that belongs (Braun and Clarke, 2006, pp. 91 to 92). In NVivo, opening a theme takes one double click.

A worked example

Twenty passages under Remittances rose after the hurricane

Suppose the candidate theme contains two codes with twenty passages between them. On reading them you find six that describe money sent every month before the storm for school fees. Those six belong under a code outside this theme. The theme now rests on fourteen passages, and fourteen is the number you report.

Why this matters
After phase three you have a tidy list of candidate themes, and the list looks finished. Phase four is where you find out whether the passages under each candidate theme say what its name claims.
Sources

Braun, V., & Clarke, V. (2006). Using thematic analysis in psychology. Qualitative Research in Psychology, 3(2), 77–101. https://doi.org/10.1191/1478088706qp063oa

Saldaña, J. (2021). The coding manual for qualitative researchers (4th ed.). SAGE. https://www.sagepub.com/shop/buy-a-book/the-coding-manual-for-qualitative-researchers-4-273583

Charmaz, K. (2006). Constructing grounded theory: A practical guide through qualitative analysis. SAGE. https://uk.sagepub.com/en-gb/eur/constructing-grounded-theory/book255601

These six phases come from Braun and Clarke, on pages 87 to 93 of the paper on your reading list, and Table 1 on page 87 lists them (Braun and Clarke, 2006). Read them across the picture with me, then answer the question: which of the six takes the longest, and which is most often skipped? Phase two usually takes longest, because you do it for every passage of every text. Phase four is the one most easily skipped, and by the end of this slide you will know why.

Phase one is familiarising yourself with your data. You read everything once before you code anything, actively, noting ideas as you go. Braun and Clarke say you need to know the depth and the breadth of your material before you start deciding what matters in it (Braun and Clarke, 2006, p. 87). Reading everything first means that when you code the first transcript, you already know what the other eleven say. You will give a code to an idea in the first transcript that you would otherwise have passed over, because you know it comes back in the seventh and the ninth. You will also leave uncoded an idea that sounds important in the first transcript but never appears again.

Phase two is generating initial codes. You work through every text. Each time a passage says something for your research question, you write a code for it. Code for as many ideas as you can, because you do not yet know which will matter. Keep a few words of surrounding text with each coded passage, so that the passage still makes sense when you read it on its own later. If one passage contains two distinct ideas, give it two codes. More than one code per passage is normal (Braun and Clarke, 2006, p. 89). At the end of phase two you have a long list of codes. Each code has the passages from the text attached to it. Different academics use slightly different words for these phases. Saldaña, whose coding manual is a supplementary reading on the module outline, calls this phase first cycle coding (Saldaña, 2021). Do not worry about the terminology as long as you understand what each phase does.

Phase three is searching for themes. You stop reading the texts and you read your list of codes instead. You sort the codes into groups of codes that are about the same idea. Braun and Clarke suggest using a visual technique for this: a table, a mind map, or each code name written on a separate slip of paper so that you can move the slips around on a desk or a board until the codes that belong together sit together (Braun and Clarke, 2006, p. 89). Sticky notes on a wall work the same way, one colour per idea. When the groups are settled, draw them: each group as a box with its code names inside, and lines between groups that relate to each other. Braun and Clarke call that drawing a thematic map (Braun and Clarke, 2006, pp. 89 to 90). On slide 13 you will see two thematic maps from one published study, the first map and the final map. Each group on the map is a candidate theme. Most groups contain several codes. Some groups become sub-themes, which are themes inside a larger theme. A code that fits nowhere goes into a miscellaneous group for now. At the end of phase three you have, in their words, a collection of candidate themes and sub-themes, with all the coded passages under them. The word candidate matters, because nothing has been checked yet (Braun and Clarke, 2006, p. 90). Saldaña calls this phase second cycle coding; Charmaz calls it focused coding (Saldaña, 2021; Charmaz, 2006). Each move in this phase is the one you will make with ten codes later today: read two code names and decide whether they are about the same idea.

Phase four, reviewing the candidate themes, is the check. For each candidate theme you open it and you read every passage under it, one after another, asking of each passage whether it belongs there. Then you reread the whole set of texts to see whether you missed a passage that belongs somewhere (Braun and Clarke, 2006, pp. 91 to 92). People skip this phase because after phase three they have a tidy list of candidate themes on a page, and the list looks finished. The card on the right shows what the check finds. Suppose you have a candidate theme called Remittances rose after the hurricane, containing two codes with twenty passages between them. On reading them you find that six describe money sent every month before the storm to pay school fees. Those six say nothing about the hurricane, so they belong under a code outside this theme. Your theme now rests on fourteen passages, which is the number you report. Without phase four you would have reported twenty, and an examiner who opened the theme could find the six in a few minutes. Once a candidate theme has been read through and every passage under it belongs there, it is a theme. The two words differ only in that check.

Phase five is defining and naming the themes that survived. For each theme you write what it is about, what it covers and what it does not, and how it fits the story the themes tell together about your question. You decide whether the theme needs sub-themes inside it to give it structure. Braun and Clarke's test is this: if you cannot describe the scope and content of a theme in a couple of sentences, the theme is not ready, and the name you give it should tell a reader at once what it is about (Braun and Clarke, 2006, pp. 92 to 93). The Money slide shows the test: Money describes nothing; remittances pay for what a household owes its family and church describes a theme.

Phase six is the chapter. You choose the passages that show each theme most clearly, you quote them word for word with their page, and you write around them an argument that answers your question. Braun and Clarke say the writing has to go beyond describing what the passages say and has to make an argument in relation to the research question (Braun and Clarke, 2006, p. 93). A chapter that strings quotations together with a sentence between each is the first failure of the method on their list, and we come back to it after the activity (Braun and Clarke, 2006, p. 94). For now, I would like to focus on how we group the codes together, since it is an intricate and important phase, given that it shapes how your themes are created.

The first day · Phase three, and why it exists

Why codes are grouped into themes

A reader can remember four themes. How many codes can they remember?

On the left, codes on sticky notes on my office wall, written while reading for the FAR-SIDS review. On the right, twelve codes from pages 663 to 665 of the Samoa study, grouped under four candidate themes. Each candidate theme carries every passage of every code inside it (Le Dé et al., 2015, pp. 663 to 665).

Why group at all

Codes are many and small; a theme is a pattern

Fifty codes with three passages each are a list, not an answer to a question. A theme is a pattern that runs across the texts, and every passage under every code inside the theme backs it. Putting six codes under one heading forces you to say what the six have in common, and that sentence is the claim.

Why a code goes into one theme and not another

Two tests, from Patton

Braun and Clarke take two tests from Patton, an earlier writer on qualitative evaluation. The passages inside a theme have to cohere together meaningfully, and the themes have to be clearly different from each other (Patton, 1990, cited in Braun and Clarke, 2006, p. 91). A code joins a theme when its passages speak to the same idea, for your question, as the codes already there.

Sources

Braun, V., & Clarke, V. (2006). Using thematic analysis in psychology. Qualitative Research in Psychology, 3(2), 77–101. https://doi.org/10.1191/1478088706qp063oa

Le Dé, L., Gaillard, J. C., Friesen, W., & Smith, F. M. (2015). Remittances in the face of disasters: A case study of rural Samoa. Environment, Development and Sustainability, 17(3), 653–672. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10668-014-9559-0

A reader can remember four themes. How many codes can they remember? Look at the left of the picture before you answer: a wall of sticky notes, one code on each, photographed in my office.

A reader cannot remember fifty codes, and neither can you. A wall of fifty codes answers no question. A reader who is handed one has to do the analysis themselves, which is what they asked you to do. A theme is different in two ways. It is a pattern that runs across the texts, and every passage under every code inside it backs it, so a theme is evidence of something patterned in the whole set and not one person's remark. On the right of the picture twelve codes sit under four candidate themes. The codes come from three pages of the Samoa study you met on the third slide, so accept their names for now: they label passages about aid arriving late, relatives sending money, what the family owes to ceremonies and church, and what it spends on food, school and the house. The four groups are candidates because they have been grouped and not yet checked.

The grouping is also where the thinking happens. To put six codes under one heading you have to say what the six have in common for your question, and that sentence is the claim your chapter will make. The three codes under the first candidate theme on the right, aid came late, relatives made up for the missing aid, and remittances rose when aid fell, say nothing much one at a time. Grouped, they say that relatives abroad fill the gap that aid leaves, which is a finding a reader can argue with.

The second card answers the question that follows: why does a code go into one theme and not another? Braun and Clarke take two tests from Patton. The passages inside a theme have to cohere together meaningfully, which they call internal homogeneity, and there have to be clear distinctions between themes, which they call external heterogeneity (Braun and Clarke, 2006, p. 91). In plain words, a code joins a theme when its passages speak to the same idea, for your question, as the codes already there, and it stays out when they do not. In the Samoa study, the codes that answer whether remittances are linked to aid, aid came late, relatives made up for it, remittances rose when aid fell, sit under the first candidate theme. The codes that answer what remittances were used for, ceremonies, church, food and the house, sit under the third and the fourth. A passage that says 12% of remittances went to church donations tells you nothing about whether remittances rose when aid fell, so it cannot sit under the first theme, however interesting it is.

The four groups on the right are candidate themes, and at least one of them will not survive phase four. The next slide takes four candidate themes like these through phases three, four and five, on an example built from my own project.

The first day · Phases three to five, on an invented example

From codes to themes: an example from FAR-SIDS

Twelve interviews in Tonga after a cyclone. Which candidate theme on the left is a topic and not a claim?

An invented example, not data: twelve household interviews in Tonga after a cyclone, asking how foreign aid and remittances together support recovery. Left, the map at the end of phase three. Right, the map after phases four and five.

What changed between the maps

Two candidate themes merged, one split, one renamed, one new theme

The first two candidate themes merged, because every passage about remittances arriving was also a passage about aid. The third, what the money is used for, was a topic, and its passages made two claims, so it was split. The fourth kept its passages and was renamed. Three households with no relatives overseas contradicted the first theme, so their passages became a theme of their own.

What the final product is

Five themes, each making a claim a reader can argue with

Each theme on the right makes a claim that could be wrong. Under each theme sit its sub-themes, under those its codes, and under those the passages with their page or line. A reader who doubts a theme reads downwards until they reach the words of a household.

Sources

Braun, V., & Clarke, V. (2006). Using thematic analysis in psychology. Qualitative Research in Psychology, 3(2), 77–101. https://doi.org/10.1191/1478088706qp063oa

Le Dé, L., Gaillard, J. C., Friesen, W., & Smith, F. M. (2015). Remittances in the face of disasters: A case study of rural Samoa. Environment, Development and Sustainability, 17(3), 653–672. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10668-014-9559-0

This slide is not a published study. It is an example I built so that we can walk through phases three, four and five on the concepts of my own project. Suppose that in 2027 I interview twelve households in Tonga after a cyclone, and my research question is how foreign aid and money from relatives abroad together support a household's recovery. The map on the left is what my desk could look like at the end of phase three. Before I explain it, answer the question on the slide: which of the four candidate themes on the left is a topic and not a claim?

The left map has four candidate themes. Remittances arrive before aid, with two sub-themes: money within days through transfer agents, and relatives who learn of the cyclone from the news. Aid and remittances replace each other, with two sub-themes: remittances fall when aid arrives, and remittances rise when aid is delayed. What the money is used for, with three sub-themes: food and repairs, church and ceremonies, and school fees. And obligations to family and church, with two sub-themes: sending is expected, and aid is shared with relatives in the village. Nothing has been checked. Two problems are already visible. The third candidate theme is the answer to my question: what the money is used for is a topic, in the same way that Money was a topic on the Money slide, because a reader cannot disagree with it. The last slide had the same fault: remittances pay for daily needs, the fourth group on the right of that slide, was a candidate theme that needed revising, and nothing on that slide had been through phase four yet. And the first two candidate themes both describe the timing of remittances in relation to aid, which is one idea drawn twice.

Phase four. I open each candidate theme and read every passage under it, asking whether the passage belongs there, and I apply the two tests: do the passages inside a candidate theme belong together, and are the candidate themes different from each other (Braun and Clarke, 2006, p. 91). Four changes come out of that reading. First, every passage under remittances arrive before aid turns out to be a passage about aid as well, because households describe the money from relatives by comparing it with the relief that came later, so the first two candidate themes fail the second test and merge into one theme: relatives fill the gap before aid arrives. Second, what the money is used for fails the first test. Its passages make two different claims. Households say that church and ceremonies were paid before food, which is one claim, and that the government's housing vouchers rebuilt the house while remittances fed the family, which is another. So the candidate theme splits into two themes: cultural obligations paid before daily needs, and aid for house repairs, remittances for daily needs. Third, the passages under obligations to family and church belong together, so the candidate theme passes the first test, but its name is a topic. It becomes sending as a cultural obligation, and a passage about the shame of not sending, which had sat under miscellaneous, now has a home. Fourth, while rereading the whole set I find three households with no relatives overseas, whose passages argue against the first theme, because for them nobody filled the gap and relief arrived after two weeks. Those passages had been coded and left aside. They become a theme of their own, households without relatives abroad depend on aid, which is the coral oval on the right. It did not exist on the first map, and it is the theme a donor would most want to read. Four candidate themes became five themes.

Phase five. For each of the five themes I write one or two sentences that describe what the theme covers (Braun and Clarke, 2006, p. 92). These sentences are not the name. For example, for the theme households without relatives abroad depend on aid, you would describe that as: three of the twelve households had no relatives overseas, so no money arrived from abroad and the household waited two weeks for the first relief.

That is the move from codes to themes on an example I control. The first map came out of three phases of work, reading, coding and grouping. Phase four did not replace it; phase four refined it, by reading every passage under every candidate theme, and phase five named what survived. The codes and the passages stay underneath the final map as the evidence. That is why your classwork asks for your codebook alongside the themes you report: the codebook lists every code with its definition and the number of passages coded to it, and your project file keeps the passages themselves, so a marker can read downwards from a theme to the words of the paper. The next slide shows the same move in a published study, so that you can check every step against a paper you can read yourselves.

The first day · Phases three to five, in one published study

From codes to themes: a worked example

Two maps of the same study. Which of the two is the finding?

Redrawn from Byrne (2022), Figures 1 and 2, with his theme and sub-theme names. Eleven interviews with teachers in Irish secondary schools about promoting student wellbeing.

What changed between the maps

One candidate theme became three themes, one sub-theme became two, one candidate theme disappeared

In phase four Byrne read every passage under each candidate theme and applied the two tests from the grouping slide. Factors inhibiting wellbeing promotion failed the first test, so it was broken into three themes. Sources of negative affect contained two ideas, so it was split in two. Recognising student wellbeing is not on the final map (Byrne, 2022, pp. 1405 to 1406).

What the final product is

Five themes, defined, named and written up

The final map is the finding. Each theme has a definition and a short name that tells a reader what the theme is about. The codes and the passages are not drawn on the map. They stay underneath it as the record a reader can check. They are the evidence, not the finding.

Sources

Byrne, D. (2022). A worked example of Braun and Clarke's approach to reflexive thematic analysis. Quality & Quantity, 56(3), 1391–1412. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11135-021-01182-y

Braun, V., & Clarke, V. (2006). Using thematic analysis in psychology. Qualitative Research in Psychology, 3(2), 77–101. https://doi.org/10.1191/1478088706qp063oa

Two maps of a published study are on the screen, the same two moments you saw on the last slide. Which of the two is the finding? Look at them before you answer. The study is by David Byrne, who interviewed eleven teachers and school managers in Irish secondary schools about how they promote their students' wellbeing, and who published his analysis as a worked example of Braun and Clarke's six phases (Byrne, 2022, p. 1394). The paper prints the thematic map at two moments. I have redrawn both maps with his own theme names and sub-theme names. Ovals are themes. Boxes are sub-themes. A dashed line is a relationship between two themes.

The first map, on the left, is the end of phase three. Byrne had coded his eleven interviews, read his list of codes, and sorted the codes into four candidate themes: best practice in wellbeing promotion, recognising student wellbeing, recognising educator wellbeing, and factors inhibiting wellbeing promotion. The boxes under each oval are the sub-themes he saw inside each candidate theme. The codes themselves are not drawn; they sit under the sub-themes. Nothing on this map had been checked. Byrne writes that the fourth candidate theme, with four sub-themes under it, was already dense and unwieldy and would need revision (Byrne, 2022, p. 1404). That map is what you will have on your desk in an hour. It came out of reading, coding and grouping, and it is not yet a finding, because no passage under any candidate theme had been read back against the group it sits in.

The second map, on the right, is the end of phases four and five. In phase four Byrne read every passage under each candidate theme and applied the same two tests you have now seen twice: do the passages inside a candidate theme belong together, and are the candidate themes different from each other (Byrne, 2022, p. 1405). Three changes came out of that reading. First, the sub-theme sources of negative affect, under recognising educator wellbeing, contained two ideas, the work pressures teachers already had and the new pressure of the wellbeing curriculum, so Byrne split it into two sub-themes (Byrne, 2022, p. 1405). Second, the candidate theme factors inhibiting wellbeing promotion failed the first test: Byrne could not state where the candidate theme began and ended, so he broke it into three themes, the influence of time, incompletely theorised agreements, and the axiology of wellbeing promotion, which are the three coral ovals on the right (Byrne, 2022, pp. 1405 to 1406). Third, the candidate theme recognising student wellbeing is not on the final map. The paper does not say where its codes went, and Byrne himself recommends writing a note each time a theme is removed, for exactly that reason (Byrne, 2022, p. 1406). Four candidate themes became five themes.

Here is what the five themes on the right claim, in plain words. Best practice in wellbeing promotion is what teachers said good wellbeing promotion looks like, and its sub-theme the whole-school approach argues that the right teacher has to deliver each part of the curriculum (Byrne, 2022, pp. 1407 to 1408). The axiology of wellbeing promotion is about value. Teachers said that they valued wellbeing promotion, with reservations, and that students valued it differently from teachers (Byrne, 2022, pp. 1406 and 1410). The influence of time claims that time pressure works in both directions: existing time pressure limits wellbeing promotion, and wellbeing promotion takes time from core subjects (Byrne, 2022, p. 1406). Incompletely theorised agreements claims that teachers agreed to promote wellbeing without training and without knowing the guidance documents, so they did it without a shared theory of what wellbeing is (Byrne, 2022, p. 1406). Recognising educator wellbeing is about the teachers' own wellbeing: pressures they already had, made worse by the new curriculum (Byrne, 2022, p. 1405). Byrne's paper is about method, so these themes are described only in passing; read his pages 1405 to 1410 for the full account.

The final map is the finding. In phase five Byrne wrote a definition for each of the five themes, chose the passages that show each theme most clearly, and gave each theme a short name that tells a reader what the theme is about (Byrne, 2022, pp. 1407 to 1408). The chapter is written from that map in phase six. The codes and the passages are not on the map. They stay underneath it as the record a reader can follow from a theme to its codes to the passages to the page. The codes are the evidence. The map on the right is the finding.

You have now seen phases three, four and five twice, once on my example and once on a published study. In both, phase four refined a first map of candidate themes into a final map of defined themes by reading every passage under every candidate theme, and in both the codes and the passages stay underneath the final map as the evidence. The next slide shows what an examiner needs in order to check how you developed your final themes.

The first day · What an examiner needs

The audit trail: memos, codebook and thematic maps

How does an examiner trace your analytical trail from raw data extracts to final codes and conceptualised themes?

The raw data

How many interviews, and how you chose the participants

If you interviewed twelve people, the examiner has to see that there were twelve and how you chose them. Then the examiner can judge whether a theme runs across all twelve interviews or comes from the three you found most interesting.

The codebook

Every code, with a definition and an example passage

Every code you made, a one sentence definition to describe that code, one passage as an example, and how many passages carry the code. Joffe prints a codebook in this form and calls it a coding frame (Joffe, 2012, p. 215).

The thematic maps and the memos

Which codes became which themes, and who decided

Which codes you grouped into which candidate themes, how the candidate themes became the final themes, what you dropped, and who made each decision. Braun and Clarke (2019) treat the researcher's own judgement as a resource for the analysis, so naming who decided is part of the method. These records, with the memos you write as you decide, are the audit trail an examiner reads (Nowell et al., 2017).

Sources

Braun, V., & Clarke, V. (2019). Reflecting on reflexive thematic analysis. Qualitative Research in Sport, Exercise and Health, 11(4), 589–597. https://doi.org/10.1080/2159676X.2019.1628806

Joffe, H. (2012). Thematic analysis. In D. Harper & A. R. Thompson (Eds.), Qualitative research methods in mental health and psychotherapy: A guide for students and practitioners (pp. 209–223). Wiley-Blackwell.

Glaser, B. G. (1978). Theoretical sensitivity: Advances in the methodology of grounded theory. Sociology Press.

Nowell, L. S., Norris, J. M., White, D. E., & Moules, N. J. (2017). Thematic analysis: Striving to meet the trustworthiness criteria. International Journal of Qualitative Methods, 16, 1–13. https://doi.org/10.1177/1609406917733847

Birks, M., Chapman, Y., & Francis, K. (2008). Memoing in qualitative research: Probing data and processes. Journal of Research in Nursing, 13(1), 68–75. https://doi.org/10.1177/1744987107081254

An examiner evaluates your qualitative analysis by tracing your analytical trail from raw data extracts to final codes and conceptualised themes. On the last slide, four candidate themes became five final themes, and an examiner reading the dissertation sees only the five. To trace the analytical trail, the examiner needs three records, which are the three boxes in the picture. The first record is the raw data: how many interviews you conducted, and how you chose the participants. The second record is the codebook: every code with a definition. A code with no definition is only a word, and a word can be stretched to cover almost anything. The codebook has three columns: the code name, a definition to describe that code, and one passage as an example. Joffe prints a codebook in this form and calls it a coding frame; the two words mean the same list (Joffe, 2012, p. 215). The third record is the thematic maps and the memos: which codes you grouped into which candidate themes, how the candidate themes became the final themes, and who made each decision.

No rule in this method converts codes into themes. You decide, and Braun and Clarke (2019) treat that judgement as a resource for the analysis rather than as a bias to be removed. You therefore write the judgement down in a memo. A memo is a note you write to yourself while you code, at the moment an idea strikes you, about a code or about how two codes relate (Glaser, 1978). A memo records three things: the decision you made, the alternatives you rejected, and what would change your mind. For example, when you merge two candidate themes, the memo says which two candidate themes you merged, why their passages belonged together, and which passage made you hesitate. Glaser called memos about codes and their relationships theoretical memos (Glaser, 1978). Your memos, your codebook and your thematic maps together form the audit trail: the record that shows an examiner how each decision was made and how each conclusion was reached (Lincoln and Guba, 1985, cited in Nowell et al., 2017; Birks et al., 2008, p. 70). Without the audit trail, the themes cannot be defended. With the use of AI, audit trails have become even more important these days, and examiners will ask you to defend your judgement each step of the way.

Suppose you and a colleague coded the same twelve interviews, and you disagreed about whether a passage on sending money for a cousin's funeral belongs under family obligation or under church and custom. If you record that you discussed it, decided on family obligation, and why, a reader can follow the decision and disagree with it if they wish. If you record nothing, the reader has only your word for the final list.

These three records are also what your supervisor needs in order to help you. If you finish your fieldwork with no codebook and no record of your decisions, they cannot be reconstructed afterwards, so it is important that you write the memos from the very first stage of initial coding all the way through to your thematic maps and eventually your conceptual models or frameworks.

The first day · Activity

Activity: coding on paper

You put the method into practice on a published article, in three steps.

Sources

Maher, C., Hadfield, M., Hutchings, M., & de Eyto, A. (2018). Ensuring rigor in qualitative data analysis: A design research approach to coding combining NVivo with traditional material methods. International Journal of Qualitative Methods, 17(1). https://doi.org/10.1177/1609406918786362

So, we have learned quite a bit about thematic analysis: what a code is, what a theme is, the six phases, and the audit trail an examiner reads. Now we put what we have learned into practice. You will do three steps on a published article that reports primary data. First, you code the article with a pen, in the margin. Second, you compare your codes with a classmate and talk through the differences. Third, you group your codes into themes and give each theme a name. After the three steps I show you how I grouped the same article, and then where your themes go in a dissertation. The next slide introduces the paper.

The first day · The study behind the activity

The paper you will code

Pacific Island migrants in New Zealand who sent money and goods home after a disaster.

Pairama and Le Dé (2018), Remittances for disaster risk management: perspectives from Pacific Island migrants living in New Zealand. International Journal of Disaster Risk Science, 9(3), 331 to 343.

Read the full article, open access
Sources

Pairama, J., & Le Dé, L. (2018). Remittances for disaster risk management: Perspectives from Pacific Island migrants living in New Zealand. International Journal of Disaster Risk Science, 9(3), 331–343. https://doi.org/10.1007/s13753-018-0183-8

The paper you code is by Jenna Pairama and Loïc Le Dé at Auckland University of Technology. In 2017 they interviewed twelve Pacific Island migrants in Auckland, Christchurch and Wellington, seven from Samoa, three from Tonga and two from Fiji, and ran a focus group with 25 more at a Tongan church in Auckland. All of them had sent money or goods home during a disaster: the 2009 tsunami in Samoa, or cyclone Winston in Fiji and Tonga in 2016 (Pairama and Le Dé, 2018, pp. 333 to 334). The picture shows the study. On the left are the senders in New Zealand. In the middle is how the money and the goods travelled: money from one person to another person, through a bank, a money transfer operator, a mobile phone, or cash carried by hand on the plane; goods collected by a church, packed in containers and shipped. On the right are the receivers, in the order the senders gave: the family first, then the church, then the village (p. 336). The Samoa study on slide 3 was the receiving end of this flow. This paper is the sending end.

You code the article itself. The article is not an interview transcript; the authors did not publish transcripts. The findings are the authors' account of what the migrants said, with the migrants' own sentences inside quotation marks. You code both kinds of sentence, and you mark each code Q for a quotation or A for an author sentence, so that later you can see how much of your evidence is first hand. What you code is your decision: read the article and code the passages that speak to the three objectives on the next slide.

The first day · Activity, on paper

Activity, step one: code the article

Code against the paper's three objectives (Pairama and Le Dé, 2018, p. 332).

1
Objective 1
Identifying the different remittance channels used by migrants before, during, and after disasters.
2
Objective 2
Appraising the challenges and opportunities associated with remittances in the disaster context.
3
Objective 3
Understanding migrants' views, needs, and priorities on how to support remittances for disaster risk management.
What to do, in order
  1. Read the article once without writing anything. This is phase one.
  2. Write the three objectives at the top of your first page, so that you know what you are coding for.
  3. Read the article again. Every time a passage speaks to one of the three objectives, underline the passage and write a short code in the margin. This is phase two.
  4. Write Q or A beside each code: Q for a participant's own words in quotation marks, A for the authors' sentence.
  5. For at least three of your codes, write the definition: one sentence that says what kind of passage belongs under that code.
  6. When you are done, count your codes, write the number at the top of the first page, and swap pages with a classmate.

One page of the article: the objectives at the top, passages underlined, a code in the margin, Q or A beside each code.

Sources

Pairama, J., & Le Dé, L. (2018). Remittances for disaster risk management: Perspectives from Pacific Island migrants living in New Zealand. International Journal of Disaster Risk Science, 9(3), 331–343. https://doi.org/10.1007/s13753-018-0183-8

Braun, V., & Clarke, V. (2006). Using thematic analysis in psychology. Qualitative Research in Psychology, 3(2), 77–101. https://doi.org/10.1191/1478088706qp063oa
