For this activity you need a pen and the article. I have printed copies for everyone in the room. If you are online and do not have the article printed, open it in Word, turn on Track Changes, and work the same way on the screen: highlight the passage and type the code as a comment in the margin.

The first step is to read the whole article once, without writing anything. That is phase one. Then, before you code, make sure you know what you are looking for. If this were a transcript from your own study, you would write your research question, or the objectives of your study, at the top of the first page, because that is what you code against. This is not your own study, but the authors give you their three objectives on page 332, so write those three at the top of your first page: identifying the different remittance channels used by migrants before, during and after disasters; appraising the challenges and opportunities associated with remittances in the disaster context; and understanding migrants' views, needs and priorities on how to support remittances for disaster risk management. A research question and a set of objectives do the same work for coding: a passage gets a code when it speaks to one of them.

Now that you have read the article once and you know the three objectives you are coding against, you can begin phase two. Read the article again, and every time a passage speaks to one of the three objectives, underline the passage and write a short code in the margin. Make sure that you write Q or A beside each code, so that we know where the passage comes from: a direct quotation from a participant, or the authors' own interpretation.

You do not have to do this for every code, but for at least three of your codes I would like you to write the definition. Remember that the definition is one simple sentence that says what kind of passage belongs under that code. For example, if your code is cash carried by hand, the definition could be: passages in which a migrant takes the money to the islands in person instead of sending it through a bank or a transfer operator. It is important that you get used to writing definitions, because when you start coding in NVivo, every code you create needs a definition, which is called the Description field in the codebook you export at the end. I am asking you for three only because writing a definition takes time.

Finally, when you are done coding, count your codes, write the number at the top of the first page, and swap pages with a classmate. If you are unsure whether a passage deserves a code, read the three objectives again; if you are still unsure, ask me.

The first day · What just happened

Activity, step two: compare with a classmate

Who has a code that their classmate does not have at all? Read it out.

What you will have found

Different counts, different names

Some of you wrote six codes and some twenty. The sentence about carrying cash on a plane when the transfer offices are closed will have several different names in this room, and those codes describe one idea, so they will sit under the same candidate theme when you group your codes.

A code only one of you wrote

Love, or obligation

Ten of the twelve interviewees said that the obligation to send is not a negative aspect of remitting, because it is about love of god, family and country (Pairama and Le Dé, 2018, p. 335). Somebody coded that as obligation, somebody as love, and somebody read past it.

What to do with disagreement

Decide together, then record the decision in a memo

Where you and your classmate named the same passage differently, discuss which name states the idea in the passage more accurately. Decide together, and write a memo recording the name you chose and why. The memo is the first entry in your audit trail.

Why this matters
Count your Q codes and your A codes. Most people in the room will have more A than Q, because most of a published paper is the authors speaking. A theme that rests only on A passages rests on the authors' interpretation, and your chapter has to say so.
Sources

Pairama, J., & Le Dé, L. (2018). Remittances for disaster risk management: Perspectives from Pacific Island migrants living in New Zealand. International Journal of Disaster Risk Science, 9(3), 331–343. https://doi.org/10.1007/s13753-018-0183-8

Braun, V., & Clarke, V. (2019). Reflecting on reflexive thematic analysis. Qualitative Research in Sport, Exercise and Health, 11(4), 589–597. https://doi.org/10.1080/2159676X.2019.1628806

Hands up who wrote more than fifteen codes. Hands up who wrote fewer than eight. Different counts are normal; a reader can follow six codes or twenty as long as each code has a definition.

Now the same passage with different names. The migrant who said that if the money cannot get through he would go himself and take the cash (p. 334) will have been coded cash carried by hand, transfer channels closed, or one relative travels for the family. All three names describe one idea, so when you group your codes into candidate themes in the next step, those three codes will sit under the same candidate theme.

Now the passage on page 335 where ten of the twelve interviewees say that the obligation to send is not a negative aspect of remitting, and one says: I remit because I love god, I love my family, and I love my country. Who coded that passage, and what did you call it? Somebody called it obligation, somebody love, and somebody read past it. You and your classmate read the same passage and saw different things in it. Braun and Clarke (2019) treat that difference in reading as part of the method rather than as an error. Where you and your classmate named the same passage differently, discuss which name states the idea in the passage more accurately. Decide together, and write a memo recording the name you chose and why. The memo is the first entry in your audit trail.

Last, count your Q codes and your A codes. Most of you have more A than Q, because most of a published paper is the authors speaking. A theme that rests only on A passages rests on the authors' interpretation. Keep your pages out for step three.

The first day · Activity, step three

Activity, step three: from codes to themes

Which of your codes are about the same idea, in different words?

What to do, in order
  1. Put your pages and your classmate's side by side. Where you both coded the same passage, agree on one name for that code. Where only one of you coded a passage, that code stays.
  2. On a blank sheet, write a heading for each idea that several codes share, and list under each heading the codes that belong to it. Each heading with its codes is a candidate theme. A code that fits under no heading goes under a heading called miscellaneous. This is phase three.
  3. Choose one candidate theme and go back to the article: reread every passage coded under that heading and ask whether the passage supports the idea in the heading. Move a code whose passages belong under another heading. Join two headings that describe one idea. Split a heading that covers two ideas. This is phase four.
  4. For each candidate theme that survives the review, write two sentences stating what the theme covers and what it does not cover, and give the theme a short name. This is phase five.
Sources

Pairama, J., & Le Dé, L. (2018). Remittances for disaster risk management: Perspectives from Pacific Island migrants living in New Zealand. International Journal of Disaster Risk Science, 9(3), 331–343. https://doi.org/10.1007/s13753-018-0183-8

Braun, V., & Clarke, V. (2006). Using thematic analysis in psychology. Qualitative Research in Psychology, 3(2), 77–101. https://doi.org/10.1191/1478088706qp063oa

Now that we have our codes, we are ready to group the codes into themes, which is phase three if you remember from slide 10. Pair up with one of your classmates. Put your pages side by side. Where you both coded the same passage, agree on one name for that code. Where only one of you coded a passage, that code stays; a code is not wrong because your classmate did not see it.

Then, on a blank sheet, write a heading for each idea that several of your codes share, and list under each heading the codes that belong to it. Each heading with its codes is a candidate theme. A code that fits under no heading goes under a heading called miscellaneous.

Now that you have completed phase three, which was grouping the codes into candidate themes, you are ready to start phase four, which is to review those candidate themes. Choose one candidate theme and go back to the article. Reread every passage you coded under that heading, and ask of each passage whether it supports the idea in the heading. Move a code whose passages belong under another heading. Join two headings that describe one idea. Split a heading that covers two ideas.

Finally, for each candidate theme that survives the review, write two sentences stating what the theme covers and what it does not cover, and give the theme a short name. The question to ask is: what is the overarching idea, and how do I name it so that the name includes every code and every passage under it? That is phase five.

The first day · Activity, step three continued

Draw your thematic map

Turn your sheet of headings and codes into a thematic map: one oval for each theme, its codes in boxes under it.

Sources

Braun, V., & Clarke, V. (2006). Using thematic analysis in psychology. Qualitative Research in Psychology, 3(2), 77–101. https://doi.org/10.1191/1478088706qp063oa

Take a few minutes to draw your thematic map from your final themes and codes. Draw one oval for each theme, write the theme's name inside it, and draw the codes as boxes under each oval. Where two themes are related, join them with a dashed line. Braun and Clarke call this drawing a thematic map (Braun and Clarke, 2006, pp. 89 to 90), and it is the picture you compare with mine on the next slide.

The first day · After the activity

One way the article can be grouped

Which theme did you make that this map does not have?

One grouping of the article: five candidate themes at the end of phase three, then six themes after phases four and five. Every box carries the page its passages come from (Pairama and Le Dé, 2018).

Four changes between the two maps
1Two candidate themes merged: carrying cash by hand was an answer to the channels failing.
2Two candidate themes combined into one: the cost of sending and the love behind sending are one obligation seen from two sides.
3One candidate theme renamed: goods sent together, badly coordinated described an event; goods sent without knowing local needs names the pattern.
4One candidate theme split, and one new theme from passages left aside: what migrants want changed became fees and preparedness; sending to one's own family rather than through the church became a theme of its own.
Sources

Pairama, J., & Le Dé, L. (2018). Remittances for disaster risk management: Perspectives from Pacific Island migrants living in New Zealand. International Journal of Disaster Risk Science, 9(3), 331–343. https://doi.org/10.1007/s13753-018-0183-8

Braun, V., & Clarke, V. (2006). Using thematic analysis in psychology. Qualitative Research in Psychology, 3(2), 77–101. https://doi.org/10.1191/1478088706qp063oa

Compare your thematic map with mine. Mine is one way of grouping the article, not the answer. On the left are my five candidate themes at the end of phase three, with their codes under them. On the right are the six themes that resulted after the review. Four changes happened between the two maps.

First, two candidate themes merged. When I reread the passages about carrying cash by hand, every one of them was an answer to a transfer channel failing, so the two candidate themes described one idea and became one theme: money carried by hand when channels fail.

Second, two candidate themes that seemed to contradict each other turned out to be one idea seen from two sides. The cost of sending and the love behind sending both describe the obligation to remit, so they became one theme, sending as cultural obligation and love, and the codes from both candidate themes now sit under it.

Third, one candidate theme was renamed. The passages about containers belonged together, but the heading was too descriptive, goods sent together, badly coordinated, and sounded more like a topic than a theme. So I renamed it goods sent without knowing local needs, which describes a pattern of sending goods without knowing what the needs are locally, rather than describing an event that was badly coordinated.

Fourth, one candidate theme split, and one new theme appeared. What migrants want changed was a topic, and when I reread its passages they made two different claims. The first claim is about fees: every participant wanted transfer fees reduced or removed in a disaster, because the family is hit by the disaster and then by the fees, and the sender is hit by the fees too (p. 338). That became the theme transfer fees hit both ends in a disaster. The second claim is about preparedness: two thirds of the interviewees wanted remittances used to prepare families for the next disaster, through saving, income generation and a community shelter, yet the same migrants said that they send when they are asked and not before, and that they would not fund a community shelter before their own families are looked after (pp. 338 to 339). That became the theme preparedness wanted, sending stays reactive. And while rereading the whole article I found passages I had coded and left aside. The article distinguishes individual remittances, money sent to one's own family, from collective remittances, goods collected through a church and sent to a village or community. Three of four migrants prefer to send directly to their own family, and the authors list as a weakness of collective remittances that they do not benefit the family first (pp. 335 to 336). Those passages say who the migrants send to when they choose, and they explain the preference for the individual channel, so they became a theme of their own: own family before church or village.

The dashed lines on the final map mark two relationships between themes. Migrants carry cash by hand when the channels fail because they feel the obligation to send as love, so the first two themes are linked. And because migrants put their own family before the church or the village, collective preparedness is unlikely, so the family theme is linked to the preparedness theme.

Five candidate themes became six themes. Which theme did you make that my map does not have? The next slide shows where your themes go in the dissertation.

The first day · Phase six

Findings and discussion

Where do your themes go in the dissertation, and where does the literature come in?

The findings chapter

Your themes, with the passages that support them

Each theme is reported in turn: its name, its definition, and the passages under it quoted word for word, with the participant and the page. Pairama and Le Dé report the fees theme this way: every participant wanted transfer fees reduced or removed in a disaster, and a migrant is quoted: “The families in the islands are already affected by the disaster, then they are affected by the fees. Then, we [senders] are affected by the fees too” (Pairama and Le Dé, 2018, p. 338).

The discussion chapter

Your themes against the literature

Each theme is set beside what other studies found, so that the reader sees what your study confirms, adds or contradicts. Pairama and Le Dé discuss the same theme two pages later: transfer costs to the Pacific run at 10% to 15% of the amount sent (World Bank 2017), formal remittances rise when fees fall (Kakhkharov et al. 2017), and a zero-fee policy during disasters was applied after the 2009 tsunami in Samoa (Le Dé et al. 2015a) (Pairama and Le Dé, 2018, p. 340).

Why this matters
Braun and Clarke call the write-up phase six (2006, p. 93). The themes you define in phase five are the structure of both chapters: the findings chapter shows the evidence for each theme, the discussion chapter says what each theme means against what was already known.
Sources

Braun, V., & Clarke, V. (2006). Using thematic analysis in psychology. Qualitative Research in Psychology, 3(2), 77–101. https://doi.org/10.1191/1478088706qp063oa

Pairama, J., & Le Dé, L. (2018). Remittances for disaster risk management: Perspectives from Pacific Island migrants living in New Zealand. International Journal of Disaster Risk Science, 9(3), 331–343. https://doi.org/10.1007/s13753-018-0183-8

The last phase is the write-up, phase six in Braun and Clarke (2006, p. 93). Your themes become the structure of two chapters. The findings chapter reports each theme in turn: the name, the definition, and the passages under it, quoted word for word with the participant and the page, so that a reader can see the evidence. The discussion chapter takes the same themes and sets them against the literature, so that the reader sees what your study confirms, what it adds, and what it contradicts.

One example from the article you coded. In the findings, on page 338, the authors report that every participant wanted transfer fees reduced or removed in a disaster, and they quote a migrant: the families in the islands are already affected by the disaster, then they are affected by the fees, then we, the senders, are affected by the fees too. That is the theme with its evidence. In the discussion, on page 340, the same theme is set against the literature: transfer costs to the Pacific run at 10% to 15% of the amount sent, formal remittances rise when fees fall, and a zero-fee policy was applied after the 2009 tsunami in Samoa. That is what the theme means against what was already known.

Your classwork is the findings part only: the themes you found in your paper, with the passages that support them, plus the two queries. On the second day you build the codebook that lists every theme and code with its passages, which is the material both chapters are written from. Before the practical instructions for the second day, two slides on where you will use this method, and on what happens when words are reported without it.

The first day · Where you will need this method

Where you will need this method

Twelve interviews of one hour each: how many pages of text is that?

The arithmetic assumes a speaking pace of about 150 words a minute and a printed page of about 300 words.

In your dissertation

Interview transcripts and focus group notes

A master's dissertation might rest on twelve interviews or four focus groups. Each one becomes a transcript of several thousand words, and you have to read, compare and report on all of them.

In an evaluation

Interview notes and open answers on forms

Ministries, NGOs and donors ask what the people a programme served thought of it. The answers arrive as interview notes and as the open answers at the end of a form.

In a public consultation

Written comments on a draft policy

A government publishes a draft policy and receives written comments from residents, businesses and associations. Someone then has to report what the comments said and what most of them asked for.

Why this matters
In each of these places you will write a sentence such as: most respondents felt the programme came too late. A reader will ask which respondents said so, and where. The method you learned today gives you that answer: for every claim, which texts support it, which contradict it, and the passage each one rests on.

Where will you use this method? In at least three places, and the three cards name them. The first is your dissertation, which might rest on twelve interviews or four focus groups, each one a transcript of several thousand words. The second is work. If you work for a ministry, an NGO, a regional organisation or a donor, somebody will ask you what the people a programme served thought of it, and the answers will arrive as interview notes and as the open boxes at the end of a form. The third is policy. When a government publishes a draft policy for consultation, residents, businesses and associations send written comments, and somebody has to read them all and write a report saying what people asked for.

Take the first of those, because most of you face it next. A master's dissertation built on interviews often rests on about twelve interviews of one hour each. Roughly how many pages is that? Somebody give me a number before I do the arithmetic.

People speak at about 150 words a minute in an ordinary conversation, so one hour is about 9,000 words and twelve hours are about 108,000 words. A printed page carries about 300 words, so twelve interviews are around 360 pages. Your own interviews will be shorter or longer, and the size is about right. A reader does not remember 360 pages, and by page 300 they have forgotten what was said on page 41.

In every one of those jobs you will write a sentence like this: most respondents felt that the programme came too late. A reader, a reviewer or a ministry will then ask what your evidence for that sentence is. With the codebook and the passages from today you can answer. The next slide shows what the reader sees when that record was never kept.

The first day · Why a method

Why words need a method

You read thirty interviews and quote three people who say the programme failed. What does your reader not know?

A scenario, drawn to show what a reader cannot see when a report gives quotations without a record of the rest.

The vivid quotation

A vivid story is remembered; twelve calm answers are forgotten

A story told with anger or grief stays in the memory. A calm answer given by twelve different people is easy to forget.

What you expected to find

You notice what you expected to find

People tend to look for and remember the evidence that supports what they already believe. Psychologists call this tendency confirmation bias (Nickerson, 1998).

The missing record

Nothing a reader can check

Without a record, a reader cannot see how many interviews a quotation stands for, how many interviews said the opposite, or who decided what counted.

Sources

Nickerson, R. S. (1998). Confirmation bias: A ubiquitous phenomenon in many guises. Review of General Psychology, 2(2), 175–220. https://doi.org/10.1037/1089-2680.2.2.175

You have read thirty interviews for an evaluation, and your report quotes three people who say the programme failed. What does your reader not know? Talk to a classmate for thirty seconds.

Your reader does not know whether those three people speak for three interviews or for twenty seven. The picture shows the problem. On the left is what the reader sees: three quotations, and twenty seven circles the reader knows nothing about. On the right is one possibility for what the thirty interviews held. I have drawn it as a scenario, not as a real study: three people said the programme failed, twenty two said it helped, and five said neither. Every quotation in the report on the left is real, and the report still leaves the reader with the opposite of what the interviews say.

Nobody needs to be dishonest for this to happen. There are two ordinary reasons for it. The first is memory: a story told with anger or grief stays in the memory, while a calm answer repeated by twelve different people is easy to forget. The second is expectation: people tend to look for, notice and remember the evidence that supports what they already believe. Psychologists call this confirmation bias, and Raymond Nickerson reviewed the research on it in 1998 and found it in a very wide range of settings (Nickerson, 1998). If you went into the evaluation expecting the programme to have failed, the three angry interviews are the ones you would notice first.

The same happens with other expectations. Suppose a researcher interviewing Comorian families about money from relatives in Marseille believes that the money pays mostly for the grand mariage, the large customary wedding, and quotes the two families who say so, while fifteen others described school fees and medicines. Or suppose a student in Malta writing about tourism jobs quotes the four employers who complain about staff shortages and passes over the six who talk about wages. In each case the quotations are real and the picture is wrong.

A method does not stop you from having expectations, because everybody has them. A method makes your choices visible, so that a reader can see how many passages lie behind each claim and which passages point the other way. That is what the codebook and the passages you learned to keep today do for you. The next slide is what to do before the second day.

Getting NVivo and choosing your paper

Why would it matter whether you can select the text of your PDF with your mouse?

Getting NVivo onto your laptop

What to do, in order
  1. Open the UM IT Services page for NVivo, linked below. The page asks you to sign in with your UM IT Account first.
  2. Fill in the request form on that page. A person at IT Services approves each request, so it is not instant.
  3. Download the installer for your own laptop, Mac or Windows, and install it.
  4. Open NVivo once before the second day and check that it starts and does not ask for a licence key you do not have.
  5. If the page has moved, the request does not go through, or the programme will not open, email me by 12 October.
UM IT Services, NVivoNVivo 15 help, MacNVivo 15 help, Windows

Choosing your own paper

What to do, in order
  1. Search HyDi, the University library's search page, for a paper in your own research area, on a small island or small state, and filter to peer reviewed articles. About twenty pages is right. A ninety page report is not.
  2. Download the PDF and open it. Drag your mouse across one sentence, copy it, and paste it somewhere. If the words paste as words, the file has real text and you can use it.
  3. If nothing selects or pastes, the PDF is a picture of a page. Choose a different paper.
  4. Read the paper once. Then write one of your own research questions at the top of the first page: the one this paper speaks to most. You will code against that question.
  5. Email me the file name and your question by 12 October.
HyDi help, UM Library
Why this matters
The classwork asks for a word frequency query, which counts words. A PDF that is a photograph of a page contains no words the computer can read, so the query comes back empty. Reading the paper once before you code is phase one of the method, and there is no time to do it in the room.
Sources

Lumivero. (n.d.). NVivo 15 for Mac help. Retrieved September 21, 2026, from https://help-nv.qsrinternational.com/15/mac/Content/welcome.htm

Lumivero. (n.d.). NVivo 15 for Windows help. Retrieved September 21, 2026, from https://help-nv.qsrinternational.com/15/win/Content/welcome.htm

Before the second day you request NVivo and you choose a paper. Both are on this slide. Request NVivo today, because a person at IT Services approves each request, and I cannot tell you how long the queue will be in October.

NVivo 15 is made by a company called Lumivero. It is free to you under the University site licence, and it runs on Mac and on Windows. Everything you see on my screen on the second day is NVivo 15 on a Mac. Where a menu differs on Windows I say both, and the Windows help pages linked on the slide cover every step we do. Tell me now if you are on Windows, so that I know how many of you there are.

Follow the five steps on the left with me. The first link is the University IT Services page for NVivo. The page asks you to sign in with your UM IT Account before it shows you anything, so have your account details to hand. Fill in the request form on that page, download the installer for your own laptop, and then open NVivo once before the second day and check that it starts. The fifth step matters as much as the other four. If the page has moved, the request does not go through, or the programme will not open, email me by 12 October. I can sort out a licence problem in the first half of October. I cannot sort one out at one o'clock on the second day with twenty of you in the room.

Now the paper. Search HyDi, the University library's search page, for a paper in your own research area, on a small island or small state, and filter to peer reviewed articles. Pick a paper that you want to read, because you will read it closely twice and then write 400 to 500 words about it. About twenty pages is a good size. Then answer the question at the top of the slide: why would it matter whether you can select the text of your PDF with your mouse? There are two kinds of PDF. One kind contains real text: when you drag your mouse across a sentence it highlights, and you can copy it. The other kind is a photograph of a page, usually from a scanner, and dragging your mouse across it selects nothing, because as far as the computer is concerned there are no words there, only a picture. You can still code the second kind, since NVivo lets you draw a box around a region and code it, but a word frequency query counts words, a picture contains no words, and the classwork asks for that query. So the check takes two minutes: download the PDF, open it, drag your mouse across one sentence, copy it, and paste it into an email to yourself. If words appear, the paper is fine. If nothing appears, choose a different paper.

Then read the paper once from start to finish, without a pen. That is phase one. Then write one of your own research questions at the top of the first page, the one this paper speaks to most. A research project has one large question and several smaller questions underneath it, and the paper may speak to the large question or to one of the smaller ones. FAR-SIDS asks how aid and remittances shape wellbeing in island households, and under that sit questions about who sends, what the money pays for, and what changes when aid arrives. A paper on Samoa after a tsunami speaks to the last of those directly. Read your paper with your main question and your smaller questions in front of you, choose the question the paper speaks to most, and write that question at the top of the first page. You code the paper against that question, and I judge your first code on the second day against it. Keep a list of the questions the paper raises that you had not asked, because a paper that gives you a new question has done as much for your project as a paper that answers an old one. Some of those new questions may become the themes of your findings chapter. Email me the file name and the question together by 12 October, so that I know what everyone is working on and can spot a problem before you arrive. The next slide is the readings and what to bring.

Second, the NVivo guide by Allsop and colleagues, which is eighteen pages and walks through importing a file, coding, writing code definitions and keeping memos. Two warnings. It was written for an older version of NVivo, so where the guide says nodes, NVivo 15 says codes, and the NVivo 15 help pages listed on the outline show the current menus for Mac and for Windows. And it describes a team method in which two coders score their agreement; you code alone for the classwork, and as you saw on the audit trail slide, disagreement is recorded in a memo rather than scored.

Two items to bring. Your laptop, with NVivo installed and opened once, so that we do not spend the first half hour on installation. The PDF of your paper, saved on the desktop.

Welcome back. Does anyone have a problem with NVivo on their laptop? If you do, put your hand up, and I will come to you once everyone else has started.

Today we learn how to code in NVivo. On the first day you coded an article with a pen. Today you do the same work on the paper you chose, in the software. In the first half we create a project, import your paper, make codes with definitions, code passages, group codes under parent codes, and write a memo. The second day · Demonstration 1 of 17

Creating your project

The New Project window in NVivo 15 on a Mac, with the fields the steps name
The clicks, in order
  1. Open NVivo. On the opening screen choose Create New Project, or from the menu bar choose File then New Project.
  2. In Save As (on Windows the field is called Title, and File name below it), type a name you will recognise in April, when you write your dissertation. ISS5220 my project is better than Untitled.
  3. In Where (on Windows, Browse next to the file name), choose a folder you can find again, and not Downloads.
  4. Write one sentence in Description. Leave Text Content Language at English unless your paper is in another language; it sets which common words the word frequency query ignores this afternoon.
  5. Click Create Project. The window you get is empty.
What you should see

A single file ending in .nvpx in the folder you chose, and an empty NVivo window with nothing in Files and nothing in Codes. Everything you import goes inside that one file.

Why this matters
That one file is the whole project, so copy it somewhere else at the end of every session you work in it.
Sources

Lumivero. (n.d.). Create a new project. NVivo 15 for Mac help. Retrieved September 21, 2026, from https://help-nv.qsrinternational.com/15/mac/Content/projects-teamwork/create-a-new-project.htm

Open NVivo with me. If NVivo is not installed on your laptop, watch for now, and we sort NVivo out at the break.

On the opening screen click Create New Project. If you have gone past that screen, choose File, then New Project, from the menu bar (Lumivero, n.d.). In Save As, type a name for your project, for example the name of your research project. In Where, choose a folder you can find again. I suggest a folder other than Downloads, because files in Downloads get lost among everything else that lands there, and some people clear Downloads without looking. In Description, write one sentence about what the project is for.

Leave Text Content Language at English unless your paper is in another language. NVivo uses that setting to decide which common words to ignore when counting words, and we count words this afternoon.

Click Create Project. NVivo opens your new project with a help panel about Files in the middle of the window. Read the panel if you like, then click Close. The navigation down the left is what we look at on the next slide. In the folder you chose there is now one file ending in .nvpx. That one file is the whole project: everything you import and every code you make goes inside that file. So please keep a second copy somewhere else, on a USB drive or in cloud storage such as OneDrive or Google Drive, and copy the file again at the end of each session. If the laptop fails, the copy saves your work.

The second day · Demonstration 3 of 17

Importing your paper

If you delete the PDF from your desktop after today, what happens to your project?

The demonstration project after importing, with four studies from the review in the Files list
The clicks, in order
  1. On the left, under Data, click Files. Nothing in the Import menu works until you do.
  2. On the ribbon click Import, then Files, then PDFs... A PDF imported as a PDF keeps its layout, its page numbers and its figures.
  3. Find your paper and click Import. A long paper takes a few seconds.
  4. Your paper appears in the list. Double click the paper. The paper opens on the right.
  5. Above the open paper, Selection Mode has two buttons, T and a rectangle. Click T. If only the rectangle selects anything, your PDF is a picture of a page, not text, and the word count after the break will not work; see me at the break.
What you should see

Your paper in the Files list, with two numbers next to the paper. Codes is how many different codes have at least one passage in that paper. References is how many coded passages that paper contains; a reference is one passage linked to one code, so a passage coded to two codes counts twice. Both are zero until you start coding.

Why this matters
The project file keeps its own copy of your paper, so deleting the original PDF does nothing to your project. For the same reason, fixing a wrong file on your disk changes nothing inside NVivo: you have to import the file again.
Sources

Lumivero. (n.d.). Documents and PDFs. NVivo 15 for Mac help. Retrieved September 21, 2026, from https://help-nv.qsrinternational.com/15/mac/Content/files/documents-and-pdfs.htm

If you delete the PDF from your desktop after today, what happens to your project? Hands up for nothing happens. Hands up for the project breaks.

Nothing happens. When you import a file, NVivo takes a copy and puts the copy inside the project file. The copy inside the project file is the reason the project file grows. The copy is also the reason you can move the project to another laptop with everything inside. The reverse is also true: if you import the wrong version of a paper and then fix the file on your disk, NVivo still keeps the old copy. You have to import the file again (Lumivero, n.d.).

Follow the clicks with me. On the left, under Data, click Files. I said so on the last slide and I say so again, because if you do not click Files first, every option under Import is greyed out and you will think the programme is broken. Now click Import on the ribbon, then Files, then PDFs. The same menu has Documents, which is for Word files and plain text. For a journal article use PDFs, because a PDF keeps the layout and the page numbers, and you want the page numbers when you quote a passage.

Find your paper, click Import, and wait a moment. On my empty project I am importing the Samoa study: the study on slide 3 of the first day, the receiving end of the flow you coded. Everything I code this afternoon is then on a paper you know. The paper appears in the list. When you double click the paper, the paper opens on the right. Check one setting before you do anything else. Above the open paper, Selection Mode has two buttons, T and a rectangle. Click T. If only the rectangle selects anything, your PDF is a picture of a page, not text, and the word count after the break will not work; see me at the break.

Look at the two numbers next to each paper in the picture, Codes and References. Codes is how many different codes have at least one passage in that paper. References is how many coded passages that paper contains; a reference is one passage linked to one code, so a passage coded to two codes counts twice. The demonstration project shows numbers because the four studies in that project are already coded. Your paper shows zero in both until you start coding. The next slide makes your first code.

The second day · Demonstration 4 of 17

Making a code with a definition

What will your first code be called, and what belongs under the code?

The Code Properties window for one code in the demonstration project, with the name and the description filled in
The clicks, in order
  1. On the left, under Data, click Files. Double click your paper. The paper opens on the right.
  2. Read until you find a passage that speaks to your research question. That passage gives you your first code.
  3. On the left, under Coding, click Codes. On the ribbon click Create, then Code, then New Code. The Code Properties window opens.
  4. In Name, type the code name. A code name reads as a label, not as a sentence.
  5. In Description, type the definition: one sentence saying what belongs under the code and what does not.
  6. Leave Aggregate coding from child codes unticked for now, and click Done. To read or change a code later, Control-click the code and choose Get Info (on Windows, right click and choose Code Properties).
What you should see

In the picture the code is called Remittances arrive before the aid does, and its description reads: passages saying that money from relatives reached the household sooner than help from the government or an aid agency. The Location line shows that the code sits under a parent code. Parent codes come later this afternoon.

Why this matters
The codebook you export at the end of today prints these two fields side by side, with two counts next to them. A codebook with empty descriptions is a list of words that a reader cannot check.
Sources

Lumivero. (n.d.). Create codes manually. NVivo 15 for Mac help. Retrieved September 21, 2026, from https://help-nv.qsrinternational.com/15/mac/Content/nodes/create-theme-node-manually.htm

Allsop, D. B., Chelladurai, J. M., Kimball, E. R., Marks, L. D., & Hendricks, J. J. (2022). Qualitative methods with NVivo software: A practical guide for analyzing qualitative data. Psych, 4(2), 142–159. https://doi.org/10.3390/psych4020013

We now make your first code. On the left, under Data, click Files. Double click your paper, and the paper opens on the right. Read the paper with your research question in mind, until you find a passage that speaks to that question. Leave the paper open at that passage, because that passage gives you your first code, and on the next slide we code the passage to the code.

Now make the code. On the left, under Coding, click Codes. On the ribbon click Create, then Code, then New Code. The Code Properties window opens (Lumivero, n.d.). Two fields matter. In Name, type the code name: a label of a few words that says what the passage is about, not a sentence. In Description, type the definition: one sentence saying what belongs under the code and what does not. On the first day you wrote definitions with a pen. Today the definition goes in this field.

Most people leave Description empty. Please do not. The codebook you export at the end of the afternoon prints the name and the description side by side, and a codebook with empty descriptions is a list of words that a reader cannot check. Allsop and colleagues, on your reading list, write that the importance of the list of code definitions cannot be overstated (Allsop et al., 2022, p. 150). If you read the Allsop guide, you saw the word nodes where I say codes. Older versions of NVivo called a code a node. NVivo 15 says code, and the two words mean the same.

Read the code in the picture with me. The code comes from the demonstration project, and I am making the same code on my project now. The name is Remittances arrive before the aid does. The description says: passages saying that money from relatives reached the household sooner than help from the government or an aid agency. With that sentence, anyone in this room could apply the code to a new paper. The Location line says the code sits under a parent code called Remittances and diaspora. Yours will say Codes, because you have no parent codes yet. Leave the box Aggregate coding from child codes unticked. We come back to that box when we make parent codes. Click Done. Your code appears in the Codes list with zero references, because nothing is coded to the code yet. To read or change a code later, Control-click the code and choose Get Info.

Find two more passages in your paper and make a code for each one, with a definition. Then stop, because the next slide codes those passages to your codes.

The second day · Demonstration 5 of 17

Coding a passage to one code, then to a second

Can one sentence belong under two codes at once? Is coding one sentence twice a mistake?

A selected sentence in a PDF with the Code menu open. Every route to coding the sentence is on this one menu.
The clicks, in order
  1. Select the text you want to code by dragging across the text.
  2. On the Home tab click the arrow next to Code, or Control-click the selected text. Both give you the menu on the screen.
  3. Under Code Selection, choose To Existing Codes or Cases..., tick the code you want, and click Select.
  4. If the code does not exist yet, choose To New Code... instead and make the code on the spot, with the definition. Making the code at that moment is inductive coding: you make the code when you notice something in the text.
  5. To code the same passage to a second code, select the passage again and repeat. Nothing is removed.
  6. When you are coding quickly, use Quick Code Selection...: a search box opens, you type the first letters of the code name, choose the code in the list and press Return. The Recent Codes or Cases list at the bottom of the same menu does the same for codes you used a moment ago.
What you should see

In the demonstration project one sentence of the Samoa study is coded to two codes, Aid effectiveness, delivery and critique and Remittance flows, motives and behaviour. The sentence reads: remittances interact with external aid since remittances increase when external aid is low and decrease when external aid is higher (Le Dé et al., 2015, p. 653).

Why this matters
Coding one passage to two codes is not double counting. Double coding records a passage that does two jobs. The coding query after the break depends on passages coded this way.
Sources

Lumivero. (n.d.). Manual coding techniques. NVivo 15 for Mac help. Retrieved September 21, 2026, from https://help-nv.qsrinternational.com/15/mac/Content/coding/coding-techniques.htm

Le Dé, L., Gaillard, J. C., Friesen, W., & Smith, F. M. (2015). Remittances in the face of disasters: A case study of rural Samoa. Environment, Development and Sustainability, 17(3), 653–672. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10668-014-9559-0

Can one sentence belong under two codes at once? Is coding one sentence twice a mistake? Tell me what you think. One sentence can belong under two codes. Coding one sentence twice is not a mistake. Keep that answer in mind, because one of the queries after the break works only on passages coded twice.

Now the clicks. Select the text by dragging across the text, as you would in any programme. Then either click the small arrow next to Code on the Home tab of the ribbon, or Control-click the text you selected. Both give you the menu on the screen (Lumivero, n.d.). The top group says Code Selection. The first option is To Existing Codes or Cases. That option opens a list where you tick the code you want and click Select. That is coding.

The second option is To New Code. This option has a name from the first day: inductive coding. You are reading, you see something your list has no code for, and you make the code at that moment, with the definition. Now the double coding. Select the same sentence again and code the sentence to a second code. Nothing is removed. The sentence now sits under both codes.

In the Samoa study in the demonstration project there is a sentence that says remittances interact with external aid, since remittances increase when external aid is low and decrease when external aid is higher (Le Dé et al., 2015, p. 653). That one sentence is about aid and about remittances at the same time, so I coded the sentence to both codes. I am coding the sentence to both codes on my project now, so that you see the two rounds of clicks. After the break I run a query that asks for every passage coded to both of those codes together. That sentence is what comes back. That sentence answers the question my whole review asked, whether aid and remittances affect each other. The query can find the sentence only because I coded the sentence twice.

One more click before you start. Going through that menu for every passage is slow. When you are coding fast, use Quick Code Selection, which gives you a search box, or pick from Recent Codes or Cases at the bottom of the menu. Code ten passages in your own paper now. I will come round. After that we open a code and read every passage under the code.

The Reference tab of the code Aid effectiveness, delivery and critique: the three passages themselves, under the two studies they came from

Have you coded your ten passages? If you do not quite have ten, that is fine. We keep going with the next part. Under Coding on the left, click Codes. Find your biggest code, the one with the most references, and double click the code. Does every passage under the code belong there? Read the passages.

While you read, look at the two tabs at the top of the open code on the right. Summary tells you which files the code appears in and how much of each file the code covers. Reference gives you the passages themselves, grouped under the file each passage came from (Lumivero, n.d.). In the picture the demonstration project has Aid effectiveness, delivery and critique open. The code contains three passages: two from the Samoa study and one from the study by Wood, Otor and Dornan about why aid projects are less effective in the Pacific. The code covers 0.19% of the Samoa paper. Coverage is usually tiny, because you code sentences out of a twenty page article. A small percentage does not mean you have done badly.

Hands up who found a passage in their biggest code that does not belong. If you found one, that check is phase four. You run the same check again on a parent code later this afternoon. To take a passage out, select the passage, and on the Home tab click Uncode and then From This Code.

On paper, checking a theme properly means finding twenty passages across nine transcripts and reading the passages one after another. That reading takes an afternoon, which is why the check so often does not happen. Here the check takes one double click. This screen is the strongest reason I know to keep your analysis in the software rather than in a notebook. A student who uses NVivo all year without opening and reading their own codes has learnt the programme without using the part of the programme that checks the analysis.

The screen shows you that three passages are there. The screen does not tell you whether the three passages share one meaning. Only you, reading the passages, can tell. The next slide shows you where in your paper you have coded, and where you have not.

The second day · Demonstration 7 of 17

Coding stripes and highlighting

Which part of your paper carries no code? Is that because the paper says nothing there for your question?

The Samoa study with highlighting on and coding stripes down the right, each stripe labelled with its code
The clicks, in order
  1. Open a paper you have coded.
  2. On the thin toolbar directly above the text of the open paper, click Coding Stripes and choose All. Coloured bars appear down the right side, one for each code, labelled with its name.
  3. Click Highlight and choose Coding for Selected Items..., tick Codes, and click Select. Coded text turns yellow in the page itself.
  4. Scroll through the whole paper and look for the long stretches with no stripe next to them.
  5. Turn both off again when you want to read cleanly, by choosing None in each menu.
What you should see

In the picture the abstract of the Samoa study is highlighted sentence by sentence, and each stripe on the right carries the name of a code. If you choose Coding for All Codes or Cases instead, the whole page turns yellow on my project, because a case covers the whole file; your project has no cases yet, and you meet them after the break.

What this cannot tell you. Why a stretch of the paper has no stripe. A long gap is either a part of the paper that says nothing for your question, or the point where you stopped reading properly. Rereading tells you which.

Why this matters
Attention often falls as you read: you start carefully, and by page fourteen you may be skimming. The stripes show where your attention fell, so run this check before you decide you have finished a paper.
Sources

Lumivero. (n.d.). Manual coding techniques. NVivo 15 for Mac help. Retrieved September 21, 2026, from https://help-nv.qsrinternational.com/15/mac/Content/coding/coding-techniques.htm

Le Dé, L., Gaillard, J. C., Friesen, W., & Smith, F. M. (2015). Remittances in the face of disasters: A case study of rural Samoa. Environment, Development and Sustainability, 17(3), 653–672. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10668-014-9559-0

Do this check with me on your own paper, because the check is quick and may tell you something you do not want to hear. Open a paper you have coded. Above the paper, click Coding Stripes and choose All. Coloured bars appear down the right hand side, one for each code, each bar labelled. Then click Highlight and choose Coding for Selected Items. Tick Codes in the window that opens, and click Select. The coded text turns yellow in the page (Lumivero, n.d.).

Now scroll through the whole paper slowly and ask the question on the slide: which part of your paper carries no code? Is that because the paper says nothing there for your question, or because you started skimming at that page? Look at the picture, which is the Samoa study in the demonstration project. The abstract is covered in stripes. The middle of the paper has far fewer. Part of that gap is real, because the methods section describes how the authors ran their workshops. Part of that gap is me reading less carefully by page twelve. Attention falls as you read. This screen shows you where.

One point confuses people. If you choose Coding for All Codes or Cases instead, the whole page goes yellow and one stripe runs the entire length of the paper. That stripe is not a coding error. That stripe is a case. A case is attached to the whole source rather than to a passage. You meet cases after the break. Until then, choose Selected Items and tick Codes.

Turn both off when you want to read normally, by choosing None in each menu. Stripes and highlighting are a check you run, not a view you work in. You now have a list of codes. The next slide groups the codes, which is phase three.

The second day · Demonstration 8 of 17

Grouping codes under a parent code

Look at your list of codes. Which of your codes are about the same idea?

The demonstration project’s codes: six parent codes, with seventeen child codes indented under them
The clicks, in order
  1. Read your list of codes and decide which codes belong together.
  2. On the ribbon click Create, then Code, then New Code. Name the new code for what the group is about. Leave the description empty for now. This new code becomes the parent code.
  3. Click a code you want to move, keep the mouse button down for a moment, drag the code onto the group code, and let go. The code moves under the group code, indented, as a child code. If the drag does not work, Control-click the code and choose Cut, then Control-click the group code and choose Paste.
  4. Control-click the parent code, choose Get Info (Code Properties on Windows), and tick Aggregate coding from child codes. Double click the parent code, click the Reference tab, and read every passage: phase four. Then open Get Info again and untick the box, or the queries after the break count each passage twice.
  5. Open Get Info on the parent code again and write a definition in Description: a sentence a reader could disagree with. Phase five.
What you should see

Six parent codes and seventeen child codes. Sixteen child codes came from the coding frame of my review. One, Remittances arrive before the aid does, was added while reading the Samoa study. The memo on the next slide records why.

What this cannot tell you. Which codes belong together. The software moves whatever you drag, and the judgement that two codes share a meaning is yours.

Why this matters
Grouping codes under a parent code is the same move as the headings you wrote with a pen on the first day, whether you have twenty codes or seven hundred.
Sources

Lumivero. (n.d.). Create codes manually. NVivo 15 for Mac help. Retrieved September 21, 2026, from https://help-nv.qsrinternational.com/15/mac/Content/nodes/create-theme-node-manually.htm

Now that you have a list of codes, we move to phase three, searching for themes. On the first day you grouped your codes under headings, and each heading was a candidate theme. In NVivo the heading is a parent code, and the codes under the heading are child codes. Look at your list of codes. Which of your codes are about the same idea?

Make the heading first. On the ribbon click Create, then Code, then New Code. Name the new code for the idea the group shares, leave the description empty for now, and click Done. Then move the codes under the heading: click a code, keep the mouse button down for a moment, drag the code onto the new code, and let go when the new code is highlighted. The code moves under the heading, indented. The heading is now a parent code, and the code under the heading is a child code. If the drag does not work, Control-click the code and choose Cut, then Control-click the parent code and choose Paste. Repeat for every group. A code that fits nowhere can stay on its own, as on the first day.

The picture shows the demonstration project’s codes: six parent codes with seventeen child codes under them. Your classwork asks for two levels like this. Sixteen of the child codes came from the coding frame of my review. The seventeenth, Remittances arrive before the aid does, is the code I added while reading the Samoa study. I put that code under Remittances and diaspora, because the passages are about remittances. The next slide shows the memo I wrote about that decision.

Now phase four, reviewing the candidate theme, as you did on the first day by rereading every passage under a heading. Control-click a parent code, choose Get Info, and tick Aggregate coding from child codes. With the box ticked, the parent code shows every passage from the child codes together. Double click the parent code, then click the Reference tab, because the Reference tab shows the passages themselves; the Summary tab only lists the files the passages came from. Read every passage. If a passage does not belong, move the child code to another parent code, or uncode the passage. When you have finished reading, open Get Info again and untick Aggregate coding from child codes. The box is only for reading. If the box stays ticked, the queries after the break count each passage twice, once under the child code and once under the parent code.

Last, phase five. Open Get Info on the parent code again and write a definition in Description: a sentence that says what the theme claims. The codebook you export at the end prints that sentence beside the parent code. The next slide is the memo, where you write down why you grouped the codes as you did. On the first day you saw that memos are the audit trail: the record a reader or an examiner follows to see how you developed your themes.

The second day · Demonstration 9 of 17

Writing a memo

You made a code this afternoon that you were unsure about. Why did you make that code?

The memo behind one code in the demonstration project, written on the day the code was made
The clicks, in order
  1. Under Coding, click Codes. Control-click the code the memo is about, choose Memo Link, then Link to New Memo... The memo is then attached to that code.
  2. A Memo Properties window opens with the name selected. Give the memo a name that says what the memo is about, and not Untitled. Click Done, then type into the memo tab that has opened. The memo tab behaves like an ordinary text document.
  3. Write the date first, then what you decided, then what else you considered and rejected, then what would change your mind.
  4. To open the memo again later, Control-click the code, choose Memo Link, then Open Linked Memo. All memos also sit under Notes on the left.
What you should see

Three parts go in a memo. Why the code exists, which is the decision. What else you considered and rejected, which is the alternative. What would make you change the code, which is the test. The memo on the screen has all three, and its third paragraph says that if no second study reports the same timing, the code belongs in the write up as one study’s finding and not as a theme.

Why this matters
Anybody with your project file can reconstruct your codes and passages. Nobody can reconstruct your reasons, so write the memo on the day you make the decision.
Sources

Lumivero. (n.d.). Memos. NVivo 15 for Mac help. Retrieved September 21, 2026, from https://help-nv.qsrinternational.com/15/mac/Content/notes/memos.htm

Think back over the last hour. You made a code you were not sure about, and so did most of the room. Why did you make that code? Will you still know the answer in April? Two months after I make a code I often cannot say why I made the code. So now I write the reason down. The place NVivo gives you for the reason is a memo (Lumivero, n.d.).

The clicks are short. Under Coding, click Codes. Control-click the code the memo is about, choose Memo Link and then Link to New Memo. The memo is then attached to that code, so you can find the memo from the code later. A Memo Properties window opens with the name already selected. Type a name that says what the memo is about, rather than leaving the name as Untitled, because you will end up with a dozen memos. Click Done, and then type into the memo tab that opens. The memo tab behaves like an ordinary text document. Write the date first, then what you decided, then what else you considered and rejected, then what would change your mind. To open the memo again later, Control-click the code, choose Memo Link and then Open Linked Memo. All your memos also sit under Notes on the left.

Read the memo in the picture with me. The memo is the real memo from the demonstration project, and the memo has the three parts the steps name. The first paragraph says that the coding frame I brought from my review has a code for aid effectiveness and a code for remittance flows, and that neither code covers what Le Dé and colleagues report, because their claim is about when the money came. That paragraph is the first part: why the code exists. The second paragraph says I could have folded the passages into aid effectiveness and chose not to, because folding them in would hide a claim about timing inside a code about whether projects worked. That paragraph is the second part: what I rejected. The third paragraph says that two passages are coded here, both from one study, and that if no second study reports the same timing, the code belongs in the write up as one study’s finding and not as a theme. That paragraph is the third part: what would change my mind.

Copy that third paragraph. Writing down what would make you abandon your own code is often the most useful sentence in a memo, because that sentence stops you defending a theme you no longer believe in only because you have already named the theme. Write one memo now, about a decision you made this afternoon. Then we save, which is the next slide.

The second day · End of the first half

Saving, and the four checks before the break

Saving

One file, and a second copy somewhere else

Press Command and S on a Mac, or Control and S on Windows. Then copy the project file to a USB drive or to cloud storage, so that you have a second copy somewhere safe. Make that copy at the end of every session.

What you should have by now

Check all four before the break

  1. Your paper imported, and its text selects.
  2. Your codes, each with a definition in the Description field.
  3. Your codes arranged in two levels, with parent codes and child codes.
  4. At least one passage coded to two codes at once, because the coding query after the break needs one.
Why this matters
If no passage in your paper has ever been coded twice, the coding query runs perfectly and returns nothing, and you cannot then tell whether you have made a mistake or found an absence.

Well done. During the first half of today you created a project, imported your paper, made codes with definitions, coded passages, grouped codes under parent codes, and wrote a memo. That is the method from the first day, now in the software.

Before we break, four quick checks. One, your paper is imported. Two, your codes have definitions in the Description field. Three, your codes are in two levels, parent codes and child codes. Four, at least one passage is coded to two codes at once. The fourth check matters for after the break: the coding query looks for passages coded to two codes, and if your paper has no such passage, the query returns nothing. If you have no passage coded twice, find a sentence that speaks to two of your codes and code the sentence to both.

Then save your work. Press Command and S on a Mac, or Control and S on Windows. Copy the project file to a USB drive or to cloud storage, so that you have a second copy somewhere safe. See you after the break.

The second day · 16 October 2026 · Second half

Turning coded text into answers

Four queries, three charts, and your codebook

How this half runsI run each query on the demonstration project first, which has four coded studies. Then you run the same query on your own paper. Cases and the crosstab need more than one source, so those two you watch.
The four queries

Two count words, and two count your coding

Word frequency and text search count words. The coding query and the crosstab count your coding.

The three charts

Each one shows something, and hides something

The word cloud, the word tree and the hierarchy chart draw a result as a picture. Each one shows one thing and hides the rest.

Sources

Welcome back. In the first half you coded your paper. In this half we ask NVivo questions about the coded text. NVivo calls a question a query. I run each query on the demonstration project first, because a query needs coded text to work on, and the demonstration project has four coded studies. Then you run the same query on your own paper. Two queries, cases and the crosstab, need more than one source, so those two you watch.

Two queries count words: word frequency and text search. A word count does not care whether you coded anything. Two queries count your coding: the coding query and the crosstab. Those two only work if your coding is careful. After each query, ask what the result can and cannot tell you. The next slide is the first query, which counts words.

The second day · Demonstration 10 of 17

The word frequency query

Before I run the query: which word do you think comes first in four studies about aid and remittances?

The result on the four studies, with the Similar Words column showing what was counted together
The clicks, in order
  1. On the ribbon click Explore, then Word Frequency.
  2. Leave Search in on Files and Externals to search everything, or choose Selected Items to search one paper.
  3. Under Finding matches, choose Include stemmed words. Stemming counts remit, remits, remitted and remittances as one word instead of four.
  4. At Display words, choose 50 most frequent rather than All, and click Run Query.
  5. Read the Similar Words column on the right, which tells you exactly which words were counted together.
  6. For a junk word such as wiley or https, Control-click the word, choose Add to Stop Words List, and click Run Query again.
What you should see
remittances492project255
households252effects231
pacific205aid192
wiley150https137

What this cannot tell you. What any of these words means in context, or whether a paper agrees or disagrees with a claim.

Sources

Lumivero. (n.d.). Word frequency query. NVivo 15 for Mac help. Retrieved September 21, 2026, from https://help-nv.qsrinternational.com/15/mac/Content/queries/word-frequency-query.htm

Guess before I run the query: four studies about aid and remittances, which word comes first? Remittances, of course. A word count tells you what is frequent, not what matters.

Click Explore, then Word Frequency. Three settings (Lumivero, n.d.). Search in: leave Files and Externals, which searches everything. Finding matches: choose Include stemmed words, so that remit, remits, remitted and remittances count as one word. Display words: choose 50 most frequent. Click Run Query. Read the result with me: remittances 492, project 255, households 252, effects 231, pacific 205, aid 192.

Now look further down: wiley 150 and https 137. Wiley is the publisher. Https starts every web address in the reference lists. Neither word has anything to do with aid or remittances, and a word cloud with the publisher’s name in large letters tells an examiner that you never looked at your own output. Remove the two words: Control-click wiley in the list, choose Add to Stop Words List, do the same for https, and click Run Query again.

The Similar Words column on the right shows which words were counted together, so if something looks strange, look there. Run the query on your own paper now with the same settings, remove the junk words, run the query again, and take a screenshot of the Summary tab. Your classwork reports that second run. The next slide draws the same result as a picture.

Text search and the word tree

The word support appears 152 times in these four studies. Does the word always carry the same meaning?

The clicks, in order
  1. On the ribbon click Explore, then Text Search.
  2. Under Search in, choose Selected Items and tick the files to search: your paper.
  3. Type the word in Search for. A phrase goes in quotation marks.
  4. Choose Include stemmed words, so that supports and supported count too, and click Run Query.
