The second day · Demonstration 13 of 17

The coding query

Which two of your own codes would be interesting to find together in one passage?

The clicks, in order
  1. Choose two codes that would be interesting to find together in one passage. Before the break you coded a passage to two codes, so you already have your pair. On the demonstration project: Aid effectiveness, delivery and critique, and Remittance flows, motives and behaviour.
  2. On the ribbon click Explore, then Queries, then Coding...
  3. On the row that says Coded to, leave the menu on all of these codes, which means a passage must carry both codes.
  4. On the same row, click the small round button at the right. A list of your codes opens. Expand the parent codes, tick your two codes and nothing else, not the parent code and no third code, and click Select.
  5. Click Run Query and read the Reference tab. Each result names the file the passage came from and gives you the passage.
What you should see

Asking for Aid effectiveness, delivery and critique together with Remittance flows, motives and behaviour returns one passage, from Le Dé and colleagues (2015, p. 653): remittances interact with external aid since remittances increase when external aid is low and decrease when external aid is higher.

What this allows you to say. One passage in one article describes aid and remittances as affecting each other, so the claim stays inside that count: one of four articles. When more sources return the pattern, the claim grows, and you report how many.

Why this matters
The coding query gives an exact count of the sources that carry a pattern, and the passages behind the count. State the count and keep the claim inside the count. An examiner reads for that.
Sources

Lumivero. (n.d.). Coding query. NVivo 15 for Mac help. Retrieved September 21, 2026, from https://help-nv.qsrinternational.com/15/mac/Content/queries/coding-query.htm

Le Dé, L., Gaillard, J. C., Friesen, W., & Smith, F. M. (2015). Remittances in the face of disasters: A case study of rural Samoa. Environment, Development and Sustainability, 17(3), 653–672. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10668-014-9559-0

The coding query finds passages coded to two codes at once. Your classwork asks for this query. First choose the two codes. On my project I choose Aid effectiveness, delivery and critique and Remittance flows, motives and behaviour, because the question behind my review is whether aid and remittances affect each other, and a passage coded to both would speak to that question. Look at your own list of codes. Before the break you coded at least one passage to two codes, so you already have your pair: those two codes are the ones to tick.

Click Explore, then Queries, then Coding (Lumivero, n.d.). On the row Coded to, leave the menu on all of these codes, which means a passage must carry both codes. Click the round button at the right of that row. Your codes appear in a list. Expand the parent codes to reach the child codes. Tick your two codes and nothing else: not the parent code, and no third code, because with all of these codes every ticked code must be on the same passage. Click Select, and click Run Query.

On my screen one passage comes back, from the Samoa study: remittances interact with external aid since remittances increase when external aid is low and decrease when external aid is higher (Le Dé et al., 2015, p. 653). That one sentence speaks to my question, and the query found the sentence in seconds. The query could find the sentence only because I coded the sentence to both codes before the break.

What does this result allow you to say? The query found one passage, in one article, that is coded to both codes. That is a fact about your sample, and you can report the fact exactly as it stands: in one of the four articles, the authors describe remittances and aid as affecting each other. What the result does not yet allow is a general claim, such as remittances and aid interact in small island states, because one passage from one article is behind the claim. The claim grows when the pattern recurs: if you run the same query on twenty interviews and twelve of them contain a passage coded to both codes, you report twelve of twenty, and the reader can judge how common the pattern is. The strength of the coding query is that the query gives you the exact count and the exact passages, so you can state how many sources carry the pattern and quote the passages. The weakness is yours to manage, not the tool’s: the number of sources behind the result decides how far the claim may go, and an examiner reads for whether you stated that number and kept the claim inside the number. Run your own query now. If nothing comes back, no passage in your paper is coded to both codes, so find a passage that speaks to both and code the passage twice. The next two demonstrations need more than one source. If you have imported more than one paper, follow along with your own project; otherwise, watch.

The second day · Demonstration 14 of 17 · Watch this one, because the step needs more than one source

Cases and attributes

You have coded a theme. How would you find out whether the theme appears more in one kind of source than in another?

The clicks, in order
  1. In Excel or Numbers: one row per source, the source name first, one fact per column. Save as csv.
  2. On the ribbon click Import, then Classifications, then Classification Sheet, and choose the file.
  3. At step 2, set Case Classification. Choose Create new classification and type a name: Study for papers, Participant for interviews. Click Next.
  4. At step 3, click Next. At step 4, click Import.
  5. Click the Classification Sheet tab to see one row per source with the facts filled in.
  6. Attach each case to its source: click one paper under Files, then Home, Code, Code Files, To Existing Codes or Cases. Click Cases, tick the case with the same name as the paper, click Select. Repeat for each paper.
After step 6: the paper is attached to its case
Why this matters
A case tells NVivo who said what. Once each case is attached to its source, every coded passage carries that source’s facts, and the crosstab can count a theme by region, gender, age or anything else you recorded.
Sources

Lumivero. (n.d.). About classifications. NVivo 15 for Mac help. Retrieved September 21, 2026, from https://help-nv.qsrinternational.com/15/mac/Content/classifications/about-classifications.htm

Your dissertation may have twelve interviews. How would you find out whether a theme appears more among the women you interviewed than among the men? NVivo knows nothing about your sources except their file names. So we tell NVivo who each source is. A case is a source with facts attached, and NVivo calls each fact an attribute. For interviews the facts might be gender, age and village. In my project each study is a case with four attributes: region, flow studied, kind of evidence, and year.

Make the facts in a spreadsheet, in Excel or Numbers, outside NVivo: one row per source, the source name in the first column exactly as NVivo shows the name under Files, one fact in each other column. Save the file as csv. In NVivo click Import, Classifications, Classification Sheet, and choose the file (Lumivero, n.d.). A window with four numbered steps opens. At step 2, set Classification type to Case Classification. Under For text files, choose Create new classification and type a name for what the cases are: Study for papers, Participant for interviews. If the classification already exists, as Study does on my project, choose Import to existing classification instead. Tick Create new attributes if they do not exist, and leave the other two boxes unticked. Click Next. At step 3, NVivo has already read your case names from the file, so the two options are greyed out. Tick Create new cases if they do not exist, and click Next. Step 4 cannot be changed in this version. Click Import.

NVivo opens the classification on the Attributes tab, which lists your columns. Click the Classification Sheet tab next to it to see the table: one row per source, with the facts filled in. Your cases also appear under Cases on the left.

One more step, and without this step the facts are not connected to any passage: attach each case to its source. Under Files, click one paper so that the row is selected. On the Home tab click Code, then Code Files, then To Existing Codes or Cases. In the window, click Cases on the left, tick the case with the same name as the paper, and click Select. A green message appears at the bottom left: Coded to, and the name of the case. Repeat for each paper.

Now think of your own interviews. Each interview is one file. You make a spreadsheet with one row per interview and a column Gender. NVivo turns each row into a case with the attribute Gender, woman or man. You attach each case to its interview file. From then on every passage you code in that interview carries the gender of the person who said it, and the crosstab on the next slide counts, for each theme, how many coded passages came from women and how many from men. Without the attach step the facts float on their own and no query can use them. Record these facts while you collect your data, when you still know them.

The second day · Demonstration 15 of 17 · Watch this one, because the query needs more than one source

The crosstab query

Three of these studies are about the Pacific and one is about the Caribbean. What can you safely say from that?

The clicks, in order
  1. On the ribbon click Explore, then Queries, then Crosstab...
  2. Under Codes, click +. A window opens. On the left, tick the box beside Codes, which ticks every parent and child code. Click Select. The codes are listed in the query.
  3. Under Show code against, leave Attributes chosen. Under Classification choose the kind of case you made, here Study.
  4. Under Attributes, set the first menu to the fact across the columns, here Region. The second menu adds a second fact, for example Gender and Age group, so that the columns show every combination.
  5. Click Run Query.
  6. The query panel is on the right of the screen. At the top of the panel click Results. Under Show results as choose Coding references and a Heat map.
Why this matters
Under each region, n is the number of articles about that region: three Pacific, one Caribbean. The Pacific column is fuller before the regions differ at all. Report the imbalance and limit the claim: an examiner looks for an interpretation that matches what the sample allows.
Sources

Lumivero. (n.d.). Crosstab query. NVivo 15 for Mac help. Retrieved September 22, 2026, from https://help-nv.qsrinternational.com/15/mac/Content/queries/crosstab-query.htm

Le Dé, L., Gaillard, J. C., Friesen, W., & Smith, F. M. (2015). Remittances in the face of disasters: A case study of rural Samoa. Environment, Development and Sustainability, 17(3), 653–672. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10668-014-9559-0

Quashie, N. T. (2019). Social welfare and remittances to older adults in two Caribbean cities. International Migration, 57(5), 71–88. https://doi.org/10.1111/imig.12591

A crosstab is a table. The rows are your codes. The columns are a fact you recorded about your sources. Each cell counts the coded passages where the two meet. In my project the fact is Region, so the columns are Pacific and Caribbean. In your interviews the fact can be Gender, so the columns are women and men.

The clicks. On the ribbon click Explore, then Queries, then Crosstab (Lumivero, n.d.). The first time, a help panel opens on the right; close the panel. Under Codes click the plus sign. A window opens with the codes of your project. On the left, tick the box beside Codes. Every parent and child code in the list is ticked. Click Select at the bottom right. The window closes and the codes are listed under Codes in the query. Under Show code against, leave Attributes chosen. Under Classification choose Study. Under Attributes, the first menu is the fact you want across the columns: choose Region. The second menu is empty, and today you leave the second menu empty. If you choose a second fact, for example Gender and Age group, the columns become every combination: women under 30, women over 30, men under 30, men over 30. That table shows whether a theme appears with one combination more than with another. Click Run Query. The query panel is on the right of the screen. At the top of that panel click the Results tab. Under Show results as choose Coding references, which counts passages, and choose a green heat map, so that the pattern is visible.

Read the table. The rows are your codes. The first two columns of numbers are the two regions, Pacific and Caribbean. Under each region, n is the number of articles about that region: n=3 means three articles are about the Pacific, n=1 means one article is about the Caribbean. Now read one row. Aid effectiveness has three passages in the Pacific column and no passages in the Caribbean column. The temptation is to write that Caribbean research does not examine aid effectiveness. That claim would be wrong, because the sample is unbalanced: three articles feed the Pacific column and one article feeds the Caribbean column, so the Pacific column has three times the opportunity to contain any theme. The difference between the columns reflects how many articles you read about each region, before it reflects anything about the regions. Used well, the crosstab is a strong tool. With a balanced sample, say five articles on each region, a difference between the columns is evidence about the literature. With an unbalanced sample, the table still shows you where your passages come from, and the correct move is to report the imbalance and limit your claim: in this sample, aid effectiveness appears only in the Pacific articles, and the sample contains one Caribbean article. An examiner is not looking for a tool that proves a point. An examiner is looking for an analyst who knows what the tool counts, what the sample allows, and who states the limit before the reader finds the limit. That is what critical thinking looks like in an analysis chapter: an interpretation that matches the data, with the assumptions that would have overreached named and set aside. Check the count two ways. In the Codes list on the left of the screen, the References column gives the number of passages in each code, and those numbers add up to 44 across the 23 codes. In the crosstab, the Total column gives 44 as well, and the two region columns, 36 and 8, add up to 44. Every coded passage in the project is in the table.

Now look at three rows that were empty when I first ran this query: Church, Gender and Food. I was tempted to write that four studies about money between family members never discuss church giving, gender or food. I went back to the text. The Samoa study says 12% of remittances went to church donations and 13% to food, and Quashie reports that migrant children in Bridgetown were less likely to send to fathers than to mothers (Le Dé et al., 2015, pp. 664 to 665; Quashie, 2019, p. 80). The rows were empty because I had not coded those passages. An empty row is a question you take back to the paper, not a finding about absence. The last chart shows which of your codes contain the most text.

The second day · Demonstration 16 of 17

The hierarchy chart

Which of your codes do you think contains the most text? Are you about to be wrong?

The clicks, in order
  1. On the ribbon click Explore, then Hierarchy Chart.
  2. Under Visualize, leave Coding for Codes chosen.
  3. On the right, under Size by, choose Coding references to size the blocks by passages, or Items coded to size the blocks by sources. Look at both.
  4. Switch between Treemap and Sunburst at the top. Rest the pointer on any block to see the code name and its counts.
  5. To use the chart in a document, Control-click the chart and choose Export.
What you should see

Rest the pointer on Livelihood strategies and household economy: Coding references 5 direct, 5 aggregate; Items coded 2 direct, 2 aggregate. Five passages, in two of the four articles. Direct is the code itself; aggregate adds its child codes.

What this allows you to say. A block is a count: passages under Coding references, sources under Items coded. A large block is a large count, not an important theme. Report the count with its unit.

Why this matters
Fifteen passages from one interview and eight passages from eight interviews are different findings: one person spoke at length, or eight people raised the theme. Say which count you are reporting, and read the passages before you report the code.
Sources

Lumivero. (n.d.). Hierarchy charts. NVivo 15 for Mac help. Retrieved September 22, 2026, from https://help-nv.qsrinternational.com/15/mac/Content/vizualizations/hierarchy-charts.htm

Guess: which of your codes contains the most text? Click Explore, then Hierarchy Chart (Lumivero, n.d.). You get a treemap. Each parent code is a large block with its name in the top left corner, and the child codes are the smaller blocks inside. The size of a block follows the number of passages coded to that code: a code with ten passages gets a block twice the size of a code with five passages. On my screen the largest block is Livelihoods and wellbeing, and inside that block the largest child code is Livelihood strategies and household economy. To see the number, rest the pointer on the block. A small box appears with Coding references 5, so that code contains five passages. The same number is in the References column of the Codes list on the left of the screen.

The box gives two counts, and each count appears twice. Coding references is the number of passages. Items coded is the number of sources that contain at least one of those passages: 2 means two of the four articles. Direct counts only the passages coded to this code itself. Aggregate adds the passages coded to its child codes. A child code has no children, so direct and aggregate are the same number. For a parent code, aggregate is larger, because the parent collects the children.

On the right, under Size by, you choose which count sets the size of the blocks. With Coding references, a block grows with the number of passages. With Items coded, a block grows with the number of sources. Click Items coded now and watch the green group. Under Coding references, Livelihood strategies and household economy was the largest block in the group, with five passages, and Poverty and inequality was clearly smaller, with two passages. Under Items coded the two blocks are the same size. Both codes appear in two of the four articles, so when the chart counts articles instead of passages, the five-passage code and the two-passage code are equal. The five passages in Livelihood strategies come from only two articles: one or both of those articles say a lot about livelihood strategies, and the other two articles say nothing about them. Poverty and inequality is mentioned by the same number of articles, once each. Health and education stays the largest block on the right, because its three passages are spread over two articles as well, and Food security stays the smallest in both views, because its two passages come from a single article. So the first chart answers the question: to which code did I code the most text? The answer is Livelihood strategies. The second chart answers a different question: which codes appear across the most articles? The answer is Poverty, Health and Livelihood strategies equally, each in two of four. If you wrote that livelihood strategies dominate the literature after looking at the first chart, the second chart shows that the claim rests on two articles.

The same difference matters with interviews. Suppose a code has fifteen passages, all from one interview. Under Coding references the block is large, because fifteen is a high count. Under Items coded the block is small, because only one person spoke about the theme. Now suppose another code has eight passages, one from each of eight interviews. Under Coding references the block is smaller than the first, because eight is less than fifteen. Under Items coded the block is larger, because eight people raised the theme. The first code tells you that one participant cared a great deal about a topic. The second tells you that a topic was shared across the group. Switch between the two settings and watch which blocks change size, because those are the codes where the two stories differ.

Next to Treemap, at the top, is the Sunburst tab. The sunburst shows the same counts as rings: the parent codes form the inner ring, the child codes form the outer ring, and the width of each wedge follows its count. Rectangles are easier to compare by eye than wedges, so the treemap is the better chart for comparing sizes; the sunburst shows the parent and child levels more clearly. Both are correct, and the choice is yours.

What does a large block allow you to say? A large block means a large count, of passages or of sources, and nothing more. A large block does not mean the theme is important, and a small block does not mean the theme is unimportant: one passage can carry the key finding of a study. Before you report a large block, open the code and read the passages, because the largest block is often the miscellaneous code from the first day, the code that collects whatever fits nowhere else. Then report the code with its count and its unit: five passages, or two of four articles. An examiner reads for a count stated with its unit, and an interpretation that stays within that count. The last demonstration is the codebook, which you attach to your classwork.

The second day · Demonstration 17 of 17

Exporting the codebook

If you exported your codebook right now, how many of the description boxes would be empty?

The lower half of the demonstration project’s codebook, exported on 23 September 2026 and opened as a document: name, description, sources and references for each code
The clicks, in order
  1. On the left, under Coding, click Codes.
  2. On the ribbon click Share, then Export, then Export Codebook...
  3. Leave the tick on Codes to take all of them, and click Select.
  4. In Save As name the file, choose the folder, leave File Format on MS Word (.docx), and click OK.
  5. Open the file and read the description column. Every empty cell is a code you cannot defend. You can still fix the empty cells today.
What you should see

Sources is how many different files the code appears in, and References is how many separate passages are coded to the code. Growth and macroeconomy, 3 sources and 3 passages, runs across the literature. Livelihood strategies and household economy, 2 sources and 5 passages, is two studies talking repeatedly. Remittances arrive before the aid does, 1 source and 2 passages, is one study said twice, which is a lead and not a theme, exactly as the memo says.

Why this matters
Your classwork has to include this document. A supervisor or an examiner reading a dissertation may well ask to see the codebook too.
Sources

Lumivero. (n.d.). Export codes and codebook. NVivo 15 for Mac help. Retrieved September 22, 2026, from https://help-nv.qsrinternational.com/15/mac/Content/nodes/export-nodes.htm

If you exported your codebook this minute, how many description boxes would be empty? We export now, so that you can still fill them in today. Under Coding, click Codes. On the ribbon click Share, Export, Export Codebook. Leave the tick on Codes, click Select, name the file, leave the format on Word, and click OK (Lumivero, n.d.). Open the file: a table with the code name, the description, the number of sources, and the number of passages.

Three rows show what the counts mean. Growth and macroeconomy: three sources, three passages, so three studies mention growth once each. Livelihood strategies and household economy: two sources, five passages, so two studies talk about livelihoods repeatedly. Remittances arrive before the aid does: one source, two passages, so one study said twice, a lead and not yet a theme, as the memo says. Twelve passages from one interview is one person talking. Four passages from four people is a pattern. The table is where you see the difference.

Now your own description column. Every empty cell is a code you cannot defend. Fill the empty cells in while you still remember what you meant, then export the codebook again, because the second export is the one you attach to your classwork. Before the classwork, one slide on what the software did this afternoon and what the software did not do.

The second day · Where the software stops

What NVivo did and did not do

Of everything we did this afternoon, which step did the software decide?

The sentence to write in your methods chapterNVivo was used to manage the coding, to retrieve coded passages, and to produce the counts reported. Do not write that NVivo analysed the data. Do not write that themes emerged from the software. Wiltshier (2011) sets out what the software does and does not do for the analysis, in a short open access paper.
Sources

Braun, V., & Clarke, V. (2006). Using thematic analysis in psychology. Qualitative Research in Psychology, 3(2), 77–101. https://doi.org/10.1191/1478088706qp063oa

Wiltshier, F. (2011). Researching with NVivo. Forum: Qualitative Social Research, 12(1). https://doi.org/10.17169/fqs-12.1.1628

Of everything we did this afternoon, which step did the software decide? Think properly and name one step.

The software decided nothing that needed judgement. The software did not choose a single passage. The software did not write a single code name. The software did not decide that two of your codes shared a meaning. When the coding query found the sentence about remittances and aid, the query found the sentence because a person had coded the sentence twice, by hand, an hour earlier. The software surfaced a judgement that had already been made.

What the software did do is useful. The software kept four studies, 23 codes and 44 coded passages in one file, and retrieved and counted the passages without losing any. On paper that work is slow, and I would have made mistakes. So the sentence to write in your methods chapter, and I would like you to write the sentence down now, is this: NVivo was used to manage the coding, to retrieve coded passages, and to produce the counts reported. Do not write that NVivo was used to analyse the data, because NVivo was not. You were. Wiltshier (2011) has a short open access paper on what this software does and does not do for the analysis. The Sources button on this slide links to the paper, so read the paper before you write your methods chapter rather than after. The next slide is the classwork, part by part.

The second day · What you hand in

The classwork, part by part

Which of the five parts are you not able to produce right now, at this desk?

What to hand in400 to 500 words, uploaded to the VLE with three attachments: the codebook exported as a Word file, a screenshot of the Summary tab of the word frequency query, and a screenshot of the Reference tab of the coding query.
Why this matters
Parts one to four show that you ran the software. Part five shows that you understood the result: what your query allows you to say about your paper, and where the claim stops. A sentence that names the limit of your own result is worth more to an examiner than a sentence that says the method has limitations.

The classwork is 400 to 500 words with three attachments, uploaded to the VLE: your codebook, exported as a Word file the way we did a few minutes ago; a screenshot of the Summary tab of your word frequency query; and a screenshot of the Reference tab of your coding query. On a Mac a screenshot of part of the screen is Command, Shift and 4. On Windows a screenshot is the Windows key, Shift and S.

The 400 to 500 words have five parts. Part one: what the paper is about and why the paper interests you. Part two: the codes you made and how you arranged them into parent and child codes. Part three: the word frequency query, with the settings you used, the words you added to the stop words list, and what the result shows. Part four: the coding query, which two codes you chose and why, and the passage the query returned. If the query returned nothing, no passage in your paper is coded to both codes; find one, code the passage twice, and run the query again, or come and see me now.

Part five is one sentence for each query: what the result allows you to say about your paper, and where that claim stops. The word frequency query counts words, so you can say which words are frequent in your paper, and you cannot say what a word meant in its sentence; we saw the word support carry five meanings. The coding query returns the passages coded to two codes, so you can say that your paper contains a passage where the two codes meet, and you cannot say that the pattern recurs until more sources return it. Do not write that the method has limitations, which says nothing. Write what your own query showed and what the query could not see in your own paper. That sentence is how I tell the difference between somebody who ran a query and somebody who understood the query.

Thank you

What we call our data are really our own constructions of other people’s constructions of what they and their compatriots are up to.

Clifford Geertz, The Interpretation of Cultures, 1973

Dr Roxane de WaeghMarie Skłodowska-Curie Postdoctoral FellowIslands and Small States InstituteUniversity of Maltaroxane.dewaegh@um.edu.mt
Sources

Geertz, C. (1973). The interpretation of cultures: Selected essays. Basic Books.

Braun, V., & Clarke, V. (2006). Using thematic analysis in psychology. Qualitative Research in Psychology, 3(2), 77–101. https://doi.org/10.1191/1478088706qp063oa

Allsop, D. B., Chelladurai, J. M., Kimball, E. R., Marks, L. D., & Hendricks, J. J. (2022). Qualitative methods with NVivo software: A practical guide for analyzing qualitative data. Psych, 4(2), 142–159. https://doi.org/10.3390/psych4020013

Lumivero. (n.d.). NVivo 15 for Windows help. Retrieved September 21, 2026, from https://help-nv.qsrinternational.com/15/win/Content/welcome.htm

Last slide, and one sentence to take home. Clifford Geertz wrote in 1973 that what we call our data are really our own constructions of other people’s constructions of what they and their compatriots are up to. Look at the picture while I say what that sentence means for the two days. In the middle is what people do: the migrants in the article send money, choose a channel, pay the fees. Around that is what people say about what they do: the migrants told Pairama and Le Dé why they send, and the two authors wrote an article about what the migrants said. Around that is what you made of what they said: your codes, your memos and your themes. Your themes were your construction of the authors’ construction of the migrants’ own account. Each ring is a different thing: what people did, what people said about what they did, and what you made of what they said are not the same, and your reading can be a long way from the first ring. The software changed nothing in those three rings. The software kept the record of your reading, so that a reader can see how you got from the words on the page to your themes.

Three habits matter more than any button in the programme: write the definition when you make the code, write the memo on the day you make the decision, and open your own codes and read the passages.

You have your project file, you have a codebook, and you have a classwork you can finish. The NVivo help pages for Mac and Windows are open to anyone and cover everything we did. The Allsop guide is open access and linked in the sources.

Thank you for your attention. If you have questions, please email me at roxane.dewaegh@um.edu.mt. Save your project before you close your laptop.
